31.title: Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak

mem.t: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

s: Find a quiet, comfortable place, get something to drink, and agree that tonight’s star is “listening.”
Each of you gets ten minutes to share “the thing weighing most on my heart lately.” The other only listens, nods, and keeps eye contact: no interrupting, no advice.
Afterward, sum it up in one sentence: “What I heard you say is… and you feel…, is that right?” Let your spouse confirm or add to it.
Finally, read James 1:19 together and say to each other: “Thank you for being willing to listen to me.”

lessons.title: Swift to Hear
lessons.theme: Communication begins with listening; listening is love’s first move

v: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and overflowing of wickedness, receive with humility the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.

lessons.still: Be quiet for one minute and say nothing; just listen: to the sounds around you, to your own breathing, and to the voice of your heart. Then say to the Lord, “Lord, speak; I am listening.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Quick to speak and slow to hear is the self on the throne: my ideas matter most, and my feelings have to be dealt with first. Being swift to hear means humbly returning to our rightful place: letting the other person finish, and letting God speak. People matter more than issues; understanding a person matters more than winning a point.
lessons.jesus: At twelve years old, Jesus was found in the temple, “sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions” (Luke 2:46). He had wisdom from heaven, yet he listened first and then asked. Jesus shows us that truly wise people aren’t in a hurry to prove themselves; they are willing first to be good listeners.
lessons.pray: God who speaks and God who listens, thank you for always listening to us so patiently. Forgive us for so often rushing to speak and rushing to anger, while being slow to listen. Give us gentle, teachable hearts, to listen first to your word and first to each other’s voice, so that our home becomes a place where each of us is heard. Amen.
teach: This week we begin the practice of “Relationships,” and the first unit is communication. James gives a simple principle that is not easy to live: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Notice the order: listen first, speak second, and emotions last. Yet many couples communicate in exactly the reverse order: get angry first, then speak, and only at the end (if at all) listen.

Why is listening so important? Because listening is a way of making room. When I truly listen, I set myself aside for a moment and let the other person be the center. Like a radio that has to be tuned to the right station before the sound comes through clearly: if my own program keeps playing in my head, I can’t hear what my spouse is saying. Very often, our spouse doesn’t need our answers; they need our ears.

James goes on: “for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). We think that if we speak a little louder and a little faster we will win the argument, but we end up winning the debate and losing the relationship. James also urges us to “receive with humility the implanted word” (James 1:21). People who are willing to listen to God are also more willing to listen to others. Being swift to hear starts with a soft, teachable heart.
q: In our conversations, am I more often “swift to speak” or “swift to hear”? How might my spouse answer that?
When my spouse is talking, is my mind listening to him or her, or preparing my own reply?
talk: When have you felt most that I was really listening to you? What was I doing then?
On which topics do we most often “stop listening”? How could we slow down a little when those topics come up?
acts: Today, when talking with your spouse, wait until he or she has finished before you speak
Put down your phone and look into your spouse’s eyes while he or she tells you something
Before bed, ask your spouse: “Is there anything you’d like to tell me about today?”
lessons.noon: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — Lord, right now help me listen first, speak slowly, and not get angry.

lessons.title: Hear It Out Before You Answer
lessons.theme: Interrupting is pride; hearing someone out is respect

v: A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion.
He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

lessons.still: Think back to a conversation you had today. Did you already “know the answer” before the other person had finished? Gently bring that picture before the Lord and ask him for a heart that is willing to wait.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind interrupting often lies the pride of “I know better than you.” Pride provokes pride: you interrupt me, I interrupt you, and the conversation becomes a battlefield. Humility draws out humility: when I hear my spouse out first, my spouse is more willing to listen to me, and we both win.
lessons.jesus: Blind Bartimaeus was shouting by the roadside, and anyone could see what he needed, yet Jesus stopped and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51). Jesus didn’t assume he already knew; he let the man say it himself. Jesus respects people’s voices and gives them room to finish.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we often answer before we have heard each other out, thinking we already understand. Forgive our pride, and teach us to pause, to wait, and to listen to the end. In every conversation, let us tell each other: you matter, and your words are worth hearing all the way through. Amen.
teach: Proverbs says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). That is very direct: answering before you have heard someone out isn’t clever; it’s foolish. After years together, husbands and wives easily assume, “I already know what you’re going to say,” so we jump in halfway with explanations and rebuttals. It’s like announcing the ending of a movie after watching only the opening: it spoils the fun, and we often guess wrong.

Another proverb fits just as well: “A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion” (Proverbs 18:2). Sometimes we talk not to understand but to express ourselves; not so the other person can be heard, but so we can be seen. Conversations like that are like two radios playing at once: lots of noise, and no one listening.

How can we practice hearing each other out? Try a simple method: when your spouse is talking, silently count to three before you respond; or first ask, “Are you finished? Is there anything else you want to add?” That small pause sends a big message: “You matter, and your words are worth hearing to the end.” This isn’t a technique; it is an expression of respect.
q: In what situations do I most often interrupt my spouse? What is going on in my heart at those moments?
When I speak, is it more to let the other person be heard, or to let myself be seen?
talk: When I interrupt you or rush to answer, how does it make you feel? Please tell me gently; I want to learn.
Could we agree on a small signal (like a light tap on the hand) to remind each other, “I’m not finished yet”?
acts: Today, before responding to your spouse, silently count to three
Ask your spouse once: “Are you finished? Anything else you want to add?”
Notice how many times you interrupt people today, and confess it to the Lord tonight
lessons.noon: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” — Lord, right now help me hear it all before I answer.

lessons.title: Hearing the Heart Behind the Words
lessons.theme: True listening hears the feelings and needs beneath the words

v: As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli saw her mouth.
Now Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!”
Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink, but I poured out my soul before the LORD.
Don’t consider your servant a wicked woman; for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.”
Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”

lessons.still: Consider: was there something your spouse said recently that carried emotions you didn’t pick up on? Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, open my ears, so that I hear not only words but hearts.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne, we interpret others through our own experience and hear only “what I assume.” The self-emptied set aside their own judgments and hear “what you really mean.” Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself: the Holy Spirit can help us hear the voice deep within another person’s heart.
lessons.jesus: After Lazarus died, Martha and Mary said almost exactly the same thing to Jesus: “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died” (John 11:32). Jesus spoke to Martha about the truth of the resurrection; but when he saw Mary weeping, “he groaned in the spirit and was troubled” (John 11:33), and “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). The same words, and Jesus heard two different hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord who searches our hearts, you heard Hannah’s silent prayer, and you hear the sighs deep within us. Open our ears so that we hear not only words but the heart behind them. Forgive us for so often judging rashly; teach us to ask first and understand first, so that misunderstandings can turn into blessings. Amen.
teach: Hannah was praying at the temple: “Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk” (1 Samuel 1:13). Eli was the high priest, a man of great experience, yet he saw only the moving lips on the surface, not the sorrowing heart beneath. He jumped straight to a verdict: “How long will you be drunk?” (1 Samuel 1:14). How much this resembles our reactions in marriage: we hear a tone of voice and judge the attitude; we see a facial expression and decide the motive.

Hannah answered, “I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit... I poured out my soul before the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:15). What looked like strange behavior had long suffering behind it. It is the same between husband and wife: “Why are you home so late again?” may really mean “I’m lonely; I need you.” “Whatever you want” may really mean “I feel my opinion doesn’t matter.” Words are like the tip of an iceberg showing above the water; the larger part lies hidden below the surface.

What is precious is that once Eli heard Hannah’s explanation, he changed his attitude at once: “Go in peace; and may the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him” (1 Samuel 1:17). He didn’t insist on his first judgment; he turned from rebuke to blessing. Hearing the heart behind the words sometimes takes one question: “When you say that, is there something you’re feeling?” Asking it can turn a misunderstanding into a blessing.
q: Have I, like Eli, judged my spouse’s motives based on the surface? When was the last time?
When I speak, do I often say the “surface words” without saying the real need underneath?
talk: Is there something you often say to me that actually hides a feeling or need I haven’t understood? Please tell me gently.
When you are feeling something but find it hard to put into words, how would you like me to ask you about it?
acts: Today, when your spouse is talking, ask: “What are you feeling inside?”
Recall a time you misunderstood your spouse, and tell him or her you’re sorry
Use “I need…” to put into words the real heart behind something you said
lessons.noon: “I poured out my soul before the LORD” — Lord, right now help me hear the voice of my spouse’s heart.

lessons.title: No Rush to Defend or Fix
lessons.theme: Being present comes before solving; weeping together comes before advising

v: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
As one who takes away a garment in cold weather, or vinegar on soda, so is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.

lessons.still: Picture a friend sitting quietly beside you: no lecturing, no analyzing, just keeping you company. Quietly thank the Lord, because he is that kind of God, the God who stays with you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rushing to defend ourselves is the self afraid of being misunderstood and losing face; rushing to give answers is the self wanting to control the situation and prove it is useful. The self-emptied can let go of face and control and first stay with the other person in their pain. Relationships matter more than being right; people matter more than issues.
lessons.jesus: Two disciples on the road to Emmaus were walking with sad faces. The risen Jesus walked with them, yet he first asked, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” (Luke 24:17), and then, “What things?” (Luke 24:19). Jesus knew everything, but he first let them pour out their disappointment, and only then did he explain the Scriptures to them.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, who walks with us, thank you for staying with us in our sorrow first and then opening our eyes with your truth. Forgive us for so often rushing to defend ourselves and to give answers, while forgetting to weep with those who weep. Teach us to be present and to listen first, so that our spouse can sense your presence through us. Amen.
teach: After Job suffered great disaster, three friends came to comfort him. At first, they did very well: “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (Job 2:13). Those seven days of silence are the most beautiful comfort in the whole book of Job. Sadly, they later opened their mouths and began analyzing causes, offering answers, and defending God, until Job said, “You are all miserable comforters!” (Job 16:2).

Couples often fall into two traps when they talk: rushing to defend ourselves, and rushing to give answers. Our spouse says, “My boss yelled at me today,” and we immediately say, “Well, you should…” Our spouse says, “What you just said hurt me,” and we immediately say, “That’s not what I meant.” Defending protects ourselves; answering closes the topic. Both leave the other person feeling, “You didn’t really listen to me.” It’s like someone who has fallen and hurt a leg: instead of first helping them sit down, you start correcting how they walk.

Proverbs uses two vivid images: “As one who takes away a garment in cold weather, or vinegar on soda, so is one who sings songs to a heavy heart” (Proverbs 25:20). Rushing to reason with someone or urging them to cheer up when they are hurting is like taking someone’s coat away in the dead of winter: it doesn’t help; it makes them colder and stings even more. Be present first, then solve; feel with them first, then speak. Try saying first, “It sounds like this has been really hard for you.” Or ask, “Do you need my advice right now, or do you just need me with you?” Sometimes the best response isn’t an answer but a hug.
q: When my spouse expresses dissatisfaction or sadness to me, is my first reaction usually to defend myself, give answers, or simply be there?
Do I feel that if I don’t give an answer or fix the problem, I haven’t helped?
talk: When you’re feeling down, do you need my advice more, or for me to stay with you and listen first? Can you give an example?
Think of a time when you felt I was really “there for you.” What did I do that comforted you?
acts: Today, ask your spouse: “Do you need my advice, or would you rather I just be with you?”
When you feel misunderstood, first say “Thank you for telling me,” and hold off on explaining
Send someone who is going through a hard time a few words that let them know you’re with them
lessons.noon: “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights” — Lord, right now help me be present first, and speak later.

lessons.title: Those Heard by God Learn to Listen
lessons.theme: Listening quietly before God first makes us good listeners for our spouse

v: I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy.
Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.
Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and trust that God is turning his ear toward you right now. You don’t need many words; just let yourself be heard by him, and quietly listen to what he says to you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God → self → others → tasks. When we are first heard and comforted before God, we won’t demand that our spouse hear us; when we first listen to God, we learn how to listen to people. With our focus on Jesus, our ears and our hearts are renewed by him.
lessons.jesus: A woman who had suffered from bleeding touched Jesus’ clothes and was healed, and Jesus stopped in his tracks. The woman, “fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth” (Mark 5:33). In a crowded, urgent throng, Jesus still gave her time to tell her whole story, then called her “Daughter” and sent her home in peace.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, who turns his ear to us, thank you for always listening to our voice and our cries for mercy. Help us first to listen quietly before you and be filled with your love, and then carry that love of being heard back into our home. Make us each other’s best listeners, so that our home becomes a place where we are heard and understood. Amen.
teach: The psalmist says, “I love the LORD, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy. Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live” (Psalm 116:1–2). “Turned his ear” is a tender picture: like a parent bending down and putting an ear close to a child to catch what the little one is whispering. Almighty God is willing to listen to us like that. People who know God hears them feel secure inside; they don’t need volume, talking over others, or self-defense to get attention.

The Teacher also reminds us that “to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools” (Ecclesiastes 5:1), and says, “Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God” (Ecclesiastes 5:2). Before God, we are listeners first and speakers second. Someone who regularly listens quietly before God will tend to listen better at home; someone who only talks in prayer will easily only talk in marriage too.

This week we have learned to be swift to hear, to hear it out before answering, to hear the heart behind the words, and not to rush to defend or fix. These are not just communication skills; they are a change of life. When we are first heard by God and first listen to God, we can carry that love of being heard to our spouse. You can start with a daily “listening time”: one talks while the other listens, then switch, so that your home becomes a place where each of you is heard.
q: When I pray, do I only talk, or do I also leave time to listen quietly to God?
Of this week’s five lessons, which one hit home the most? Where do I want to start changing?
talk: This week, do you think I have made even a little progress in listening? Please name one specific moment.
Should we agree on a short daily “listening time”? What time and what format do you think would suit us best?
acts: When you pray today, spend one minute listening quietly to God
Have a ten-minute “listening time” with your spouse, taking turns to talk and to listen
Write down the most important listening principle you learned this week
lessons.noon: “Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live” — Lord, right now thank you for listening to me; teach me to listen to others.

mem.t: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

s: Find a quiet place where you aren’t in a hurry, and each write down: “Lately, there is something I have wanted to say but haven’t said.”
First, each name three things you are grateful for in the other. Then take turns saying that sentence in the form: “When…, I feel…, because…, and I need…”
The listener doesn’t defend themselves, but simply responds: “Thank you for being willing to tell me. What I heard is…”
Read Ephesians 4:15 together and bless each other: “May we grow up in all things in love, into Christ our head.”

lessons.title: Truth and Love: We Need Both
lessons.theme: Truth without love wounds; love without truth harms

v: that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error;
but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.

lessons.still: Be still and picture Jesus sitting in front of you, his eyes both clear and kind. Tell the Lord, “Lord, you are full of grace and truth. Put both of these in my mouth today, too.” Hand over to him first that sentence that has been stuck in your heart lately.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When self is on the throne and we tell the truth, it is often to let off steam and to win; when self is on the throne and we hold back the truth, it is often to protect ourselves and avoid conflict. Either way, the center is “me.” The self-emptied speak with Christ at the center: when we let Jesus reign, we can be honest without being harsh, and gentle without being fake.
lessons.jesus: The Samaritan woman said, “I have no husband.” Jesus didn’t expose or humiliate her; he first said, “You said well, ‘I have no husband,’” (John 4:17), and then gently stated the facts: “for you have had five husbands; and he whom you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18). The truth was spoken clearly, but without contempt; and the woman later ran into town to tell people about Jesus.
lessons.pray: Lord, full of grace and truth, we admit that sometimes our truth cuts like a knife, and sometimes our silence stands like a wall. Renew our mouths, so that our words carry both truth and love. Let every word in our home help us grow up in you together, becoming more and more like you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: A surgeon needs two things in hand: a scalpel and anesthesia. A scalpel without anesthesia leaves the patient in unbearable pain; anesthesia without a scalpel leaves the disease in the body forever. It is the same with the way husbands and wives talk. Some people are very honest, but their words cut like a knife and draw blood every time; others are very mild, but always skirt the real issue, so the problem never gets dealt with. Paul says we should be “speaking truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). We can’t do without either one.

In the original language, “speaking truth” is a single verb that means not only “telling the truth” but “holding to what is true, living in the truth.” Honesty isn’t just about the mouth; it is about being open and upright as a whole person. “In love” is the air our words breathe: Am I saying this to win against you, or for your good? To vent, or to build up? The same true sentence lands completely differently in our spouse’s ears depending on whether it comes from love or from anger.

Paul goes on to say that the result is that “we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15), and the body “makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love” (Ephesians 4:16). The goal of speaking truth in love is not to prove who is right and who is wrong, but for two people to grow up together, becoming more and more like Christ. A marriage is like a small body, and every honest, gentle word is nourishment that makes that body healthier.
q: Which way do I tend to fall: telling the truth with a sting, or not telling the truth to keep the peace?
The last time I said something harsh to my spouse, what was my real motive?
talk: Was there a time when I told you the truth and you still felt loved? What did I do right then?
When I need to point out a problem, how would you like me to say it so it’s easier for you to take in?
acts: Before saying something true but hard, ask yourself: “Am I saying this for his or her good?”
Say one specific thank-you to your spouse
Write down one matter that needs honest communication, and pray about it first
lessons.noon: “speaking truth in love” — Lord, right now let every word I say carry both truth and love.

lessons.title: Put Away Lies; Speak the Truth
lessons.theme: Little lies slowly eat away at the foundation of trust

v: Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings,
and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator,
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

lessons.still: Pause for a moment and let the light of the Holy Spirit shine gently into your heart. No need to rush to defend yourself; simply ask honestly, “Lord, is there anywhere in our marriage where I have not been telling the truth?” Ask him for the courage to speak truthfully.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The root of lying is the self-ruled life: afraid of losing my image, my convenience, my advantage. The gospel tells us that in Christ I am already fully accepted, and I no longer have to pretend in order to win love. Change your mindset and your life will change: when I am no longer afraid, I can tell the truth.
lessons.jesus: Standing before Pilate, Jesus could perhaps have gotten himself released with a few vague words. Instead he said, “For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth” (John 18:37). Even when telling the truth would cost him his life, Jesus stayed true. Following him means letting our “yes” and our “no” be trustworthy.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you are the truth, and in you there is nothing false. We admit that sometimes, to protect ourselves, we have said things to each other that weren’t fully true. Forgive us, and help us put off the habits of the old self and put on the new. Make our home the most truthful place, and also the safest. Amen.
teach: Termites rarely bring a house down overnight; they quietly hollow out the beams, bit by bit. Lies in a marriage work the same way. Few couples tell earth-shattering lies, but little ones are common: “I’m fine,” when we are clearly upset; “It was really cheap,” about something we bought; a quick made-up excuse for being late. None of them is big, but together they hollow out trust, little by little.

Proverbs says, “Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight” (Proverbs 12:22). God values honesty because he himself is true. Paul gives a reason that applies especially to husband and wife: “we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25). If the eyes lied to the hand and said there was no fire ahead, the hand would get burned. Husband and wife are one; deceiving your spouse is really hurting yourself.

Paul also says, “Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings” (Colossians 3:9). Lying is the clothing of the old self. The old self lies to protect itself: afraid of blame, afraid of losing face, afraid of hassle. But the new self is “being renewed in knowledge” (Colossians 3:10). Putting off lies isn’t done by gritting our teeth with willpower; it comes from believing we are already accepted in Christ, so we no longer need lies to protect ourselves.
q: What “little lie” do I tell my spouse most often? What am I protecting?
Is there something I have never let my spouse know that is actually affecting our home?
talk: What situations make you feel that telling the truth isn’t quite safe? How can I help you feel more at ease?
When one of us says “I’m fine” but isn’t, how would you like the other to ask gently? Let’s agree on a phrase together.
acts: Today, don’t tell a single “harmless little white lie”
If you said “I’m fine” when you weren’t, gently say what is really going on today
If there is something bigger you have been hiding, first talk with a trusted pastor about how to come clean
lessons.noon: “those who do the truth are his delight” — Lord, right now I want to be real with my spouse and stop pretending.

lessons.title: Cold Wars and Hints: Silence Speaks Too
lessons.theme: Unspoken resentment ferments in the heart into bitterness

v: “‘You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him.
“‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.
Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

lessons.still: Be still and consider: is there something lately that I haven’t said out loud, but have been expressing through my expression, my sighs, or my silence? Lay it gently before the Lord and say, “Lord, give me the courage and gentleness to put it into words well.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A cold war is hidden pride: I won’t speak first, because I want you to back down first. Hinting is hidden control: I won’t say it plainly, but I want you to do what I want. Pride provokes pride, and a cold war only gets colder. The humble speak first; humility draws out humility, and the home warms up again.
lessons.jesus: Simon the Pharisee silently judged the woman who anointed Jesus with perfume, without saying a word aloud. Jesus did not pretend not to know. He said gently, “Simon, I have something to tell you” (Luke 7:40), and then used a parable to help Simon see his own heart. Jesus brought what was hidden into the light, yet always with kindness.
lessons.pray: Lord, we admit that sometimes we punish each other with silence, and sometimes we make demands through hints. Melt the ice in our hearts and forgive the resentment we have harbored. Give us humble hearts that are willing to speak first, and gentle mouths whose words build each other up. Amen.
teach: Some couples never raise their voices, yet a cold front keeps blowing through the house: no conversation at dinner, nothing but an “mm” in reply, a door closed a little louder than usual. That is a cold war. Another pattern is hinting: “You know, the neighbor’s husband always helps with the dishes.” We don’t say it directly, but we hope our spouse will guess. Cold wars and hints may seem milder than arguing, but they are speaking too, and what they say is deeply hurtful: “I don’t want to talk this through with you.”

In the law, God says, “You shall not hate your brother in your heart. You shall surely rebuke your neighbor, and not bear sin because of him” (Leviticus 19:17). God puts “hate in your heart” side by side with “not rebuking,” because unspoken resentment doesn’t simply disappear; it ferments in the heart and turns into bitterness. And right after that God says, “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). Saying things honestly and gently turns out to be part of love.

Proverbs says, “Better is open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5). Love doesn’t hide what needs saying; it has the courage to say it face to face, gently. Here we need to tell a cold war from a cool-down. A cool-down says, “My emotions are too full right now; I need thirty minutes, and then I will definitely come back to talk.” A cold war uses silence to punish the other person, leaving them with no idea when it will end. The first is for the sake of the relationship; the second is for the sake of winning.
q: When I’m upset, how do I usually express it: silence, a look, hints, or saying it directly?
When I use the silent treatment or hints, what am I really hoping to get?
talk: When I go silent or give you a look, how does it make you feel? Please tell me gently.
Could we agree on a “time-out phrase”? For example: “I need to calm down for a bit; let’s talk again in an hour.”
acts: If something bothers you today, say it directly in one calm sentence instead of hinting
Agree with your spouse on a “time-out phrase” you both accept
If you are in a cold war right now, be the first to say: “Can we talk?”
lessons.noon: “Better is open rebuke than hidden love” — Lord, right now help me not to use silence in place of gentle truth.

lessons.title: Say “I,” Not “You Always”
lessons.theme: Describe events and feelings rather than passing judgment on the person

v: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds learning to his lips.
Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.

lessons.still: Be still and recall the last time you said “You always…” or “You never…”. Don’t condemn yourself; just see it honestly. Tell the Lord, “Lord, teach my heart, so that it can instruct my mouth.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: “You always” puts the focus on the other person; “I feel” brings the focus back to me. Change starts with me: I take responsibility for my own feelings first, instead of making my spouse fully responsible for my emotions. The focus is not on others but on Jesus; with his eyes, I can see the situation clearly without judging the person.
lessons.jesus: As Jesus drew near to Jerusalem and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace!” (Luke 19:42). Here he didn’t list how the people “always” rebelled; he spoke the pain and longing in his own heart. Jesus shows us that expressing what we feel often touches hearts more deeply than condemning people does.
lessons.pray: Lord, we are often quick to judge and forget to speak our hearts. Teach our hearts, so that our mouths speak wise words. Help us deal with the issue rather than attack the person, and share our feelings rather than dredge up old scores. May our words be like a honeycomb, sweet to each other’s souls. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: “You’re always late!” “You never care about me!” Once those words are out, the other person’s first reaction is usually not self-reflection but a counterattack: “Always? I wasn’t late last time!” Because “you always” doesn’t describe an event; it passes judgment on a person. It’s like a judge banging the gavel and handing down a sentence: the defendant only wants to appeal. The real issue gets pushed aside, and the two of you start arguing about how many times “always” actually is.

Jesus taught, “show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15). There are three pieces of wisdom here. Speak privately, not in front of the children, relatives, or friends. Be specific: point out one thing rather than pulling out a whole list. And aim to “gain back” the other person: what you want to win back is the relationship, not the argument. This principle is just as precious between husband and wife.

Try this sentence pattern: “When… (a specific event), I feel… (an emotion), because… (what it means to me).” For example: “Last night you said you’d be home at seven, but you got back at nine and didn’t call. I felt really worried and a bit overlooked, because I had been waiting for you to have dinner.” “The heart of the wise instructs his mouth” (Proverbs 16:23); sort out your heart first, then speak, and your words can be like a honeycomb, “sweet to the soul” (Proverbs 16:24).
q: Which “You always…” or “You never…” do I use most? What is the real feeling behind it?
When I point out my spouse’s faults, do I want to “gain” him or her back, or to win against him or her?
talk: Each of you pick one small recent event and practice saying it with “When…, I feel…, because…”. The listener only needs to say, “Thank you for telling me.”
Which thing I say most makes you want to fight back immediately? How could we rephrase it together?
acts: Change one “You always” into “When…, I feel…”
Notice how many times you say “never” or “always”
When you need to point out a problem, say it privately, not in front of others
lessons.noon: “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul” — Lord, right now let the words of my mouth bring sweetness to my spouse.

lessons.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
lessons.theme: The right words also need the right time and the right way

v: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and look back over this week: truth and love, putting away lies, no cold wars, saying “I.” Thank the Lord for every small step forward this week. Quietly ask, “Lord, that thing I need to say: when, and how, do you want me to say it?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Living from the head by ourselves, we calculate how to say things so we can win; living from the heart by the Spirit, we ask how to say things so we can build up. The Holy Spirit is my guide, and he knows the season of my spouse’s heart. A one-line prayer before speaking, “Lord, is now the time to say this?”, can often head off an unnecessary fight.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now” (John 16:12). He held all truth, yet he spoke step by step, according to what his disciples could bear. Jesus shows us that being considerate about timing is part of love; the pace of our words should follow the other person’s heart.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives wisdom, thank you for teaching us this week to speak truth in love. Give us sensitive hearts to know when to speak and when to wait, and courage to speak the truth at the right time. May our words be like apples of gold in settings of silver, building up our home and bringing you glory. Amen.
teach: The same seed sown in winter may freeze and die, while sown in spring it sprouts. Words are like that too. Proverbs says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). “Fitly” can be understood as at the right moment and in the right way. Even the most correct words, spoken when your spouse has just come home from work, is hungry, and feels frazzled, often turn into a fight.

Solomon says there is “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Silence here is not a cold war but waiting; speaking is not venting but saying the truth at the right time. A practical approach is to “book a conversation”: “Tonight after dinner, once things are cleaned up, could you give me twenty minutes to talk about something that has been on my heart for a long time?” That way your spouse is prepared and won’t feel ambushed, and the conversation is more likely to stay calm.

This week we have learned to speak truth in love, to put away lies, to avoid cold wars and hints, to say “I” instead of “you always,” and now, to choose a fitting time. These aren’t just techniques; they are the overflow of a life. When Christ reigns in our hearts, we no longer speak for our own sake, and we no longer stay silent for our own sake. Our words become service, brick after brick building up our home.
q: At what kinds of moments do I usually bring up important matters? How does it usually turn out?
This week, what one speaking habit has the Holy Spirit reminded me I most need to change?
talk: For you, at what times and in what state is it easier to talk about important things? When is it least suitable?

This week, what small step forward in the way I speak have you noticed? Please name one specific thing. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one sentence of thanks you’d like to give him or her.)
acts: Before raising an important matter, “book” a time with your spouse first
Before you speak, pray silently: “Lord, is now the time to say this?”
Write Ephesians 4:15 on a card and put it by the dinner table
lessons.noon: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” — Lord, right now teach me when to speak and how to speak.

mem.t: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

date.t: A Card Full of Good Words
s: Each of you take a card and write down three of your spouse’s strengths, each with a specific example.
Find a quiet café, or light a candle at home, and take turns reading your card aloud to each other.
The listener doesn’t brush it off or say “Oh, not really,” but simply says: “Thank you. I receive that.”
Finish by blessing each other with Numbers 6:24–26, putting your spouse’s name in place of “you.”

lessons.title: Words That Tear Down, Words That Build Up
lessons.theme: Every word we say is either building up or tearing down

v: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

lessons.still: Be still and think about the last thing you said to your spouse yesterday. Did it leave them stronger, or more drained? No need to condemn yourself; just hand your mouth over to the Lord: “Lord, guard my lips today.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Words that tear down mostly come from the self-ruled life: I’ve been offended, I’m uncomfortable, I want to vent. Words that build up come from a self-emptied heart: first consider what my spouse needs, then decide what to say. Change your mindset and your life will change: the purpose of speaking is not to express myself, but to build up my “2,” my spouse.
lessons.jesus: In the synagogue at Nazareth, “All testified about him and wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth” (Luke 4:22). Jesus’ words carried grace: good news for the poor, release for the captives, freedom for the oppressed. He never used his mouth to tear people down, only to heal them and build them up.
lessons.pray: Lord, set a guard over our mouths and keep watch over our lips. Cleanse every rotten, hurtful word, and add to us every word that builds and heals. Don’t let us grieve the Holy Spirit with our words; instead, let them give grace to those who hear. May every word we say help build your household. Amen.
teach: Tearing down a wall may take a single afternoon; building one takes weeks. Words are the same. Paul says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). “Building up” is a word taken from constructing a house. Every word is a brick: it is either building our home or tearing it down.

“Corrupt” in the original means “rotten, putrid,” like fruit that has gone bad. It is not only coarse language; it includes harshness, humiliation, sarcasm, any word that leaves a bad smell in someone’s heart. Paul says to let “no” corrupt speech come out, because one rotten apple can spoil the whole basket. Then he says, “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30). So the Holy Spirit is listening to the words we speak to our spouse, and he grieves over words that wound.

Paul doesn’t just say “don’t say bad things”; he says to speak “only what is good for building others up as the need may be” (Ephesians 4:29). “As the need may be” means paying attention to what our spouse needs right now: when they are tired, they need understanding; when they have had a setback, they need encouragement; when they have done well, they need affirmation. Simply not saying bad things isn’t enough; the space left behind needs to be filled with good words. This week, let’s learn together the language that builds people up.
q: Thinking over what I have said to my spouse in the past two days, which words were building up, and which were tearing down?
What kind of “rotten” words slip out of my mouth most often: complaining, sarcasm, criticism, or comparison?
talk: What have I said recently that made you feel really supported?
When you’re tired or discouraged, what would you most like to hear me say?
acts: When a critical remark is on the tip of your tongue, pause for three seconds first
Say one good word to your spouse that fits what he or she needs right now
Write down one habitual phrase you most want to stop saying
lessons.noon: “only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” — Lord, right now let me speak a word that builds someone up.

lessons.title: Notice It and Say It: Words of Affirmation
lessons.theme: Put the appreciation in your heart into specific words

v: You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you.
As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, his fruit was sweet to my taste.

lessons.still: Pause for a moment and picture your spouse’s face. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes: “Lord, let me see the good work you are doing in him or her.” Each time something comes to mind, silently thank God for it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne, our eyes see only our spouse’s faults, because our focus is on “What am I getting?” The self-emptied learn to see God’s work in their spouse. Shift from a human point of view to God’s point of view: my spouse is not someone for me to grade, but a work of art God is still carving.
lessons.jesus: As soon as Jesus saw Nathanael, he said, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit!” (John 1:47). Before Nathanael had done anything, Jesus had already seen and named the good in him. That one specific affirmation opened Nathanael’s heart, and he recognized Jesus as the Son of God.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us to each other; there is so much good in my spouse that you made with your own hands. Open our eyes to see your work in each other, and open our mouths to put our appreciation into specific words. Fill our home with the sound of affirmation, so that we are strengthened in love. Amen.
teach: Many people truly appreciate their spouse but never say it, thinking, “Surely they know.” But appreciation that is never spoken is like a gift left in a drawer and never sent: the other person never receives it. The Song of Songs is a book full of praise. The bridegroom says, “You are all beautiful, my love. There is no spot in you” (Song of Songs 4:7). He doesn’t just think it; he says it to her face.

Affirmation isn’t one-way, either. The bride says of her beloved, “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song of Songs 2:3), and sitting in his shade, “his fruit was sweet to my taste” (Song of Songs 2:3). Husbands need affirmation, and so do wives. Some people are often praised at work but hear only demands when they get home; some care for the household all day and never hear anyone say, “Thank you for all your hard work.” Home should be the place where we hear affirmation most often, not least.

Affirmation has power when it is specific. “You’re great” isn’t as strong as “I saw how tired you were after work today, and you still patiently talked with my mom on the phone for half an hour. I really appreciate how thoughtful you are.” Try three steps: “I saw you… (a specific action); it made me feel…; I appreciate your… (a quality of character).” Specific affirmation tells your spouse: I really do see you. That is how God treats us too: he sees and remembers every small thing we offer.
q: What do I appreciate about my spouse in my heart but have never said out loud?
Do I often take my spouse’s efforts for granted? Which one stands out most?
talk: Use “I saw you…, it made me feel…, I appreciate your…” to give each other one specific affirmation.
What kind of affirmation makes you feel most loved: about your appearance, your abilities, your character, or the things you do for us?
acts: Give your spouse one specific affirmation, naming both the action and the character quality
Today, praise your spouse once in front of others
Write down three of your spouse’s strengths and save them on your phone
lessons.noon: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons” — Lord, right now I thank you for my spouse.

lessons.title: Thanks Said Out Loud
lessons.theme: Gratitude makes unseen efforts visible

v: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

lessons.still: Be still and count: what has your spouse quietly done for your home today? Clean dishes, a paid bill, a glass of warm water… One by one, say before the Lord, “Thank you, Lord, for caring for me through him (or her).”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The root of complaining is “I deserve this”; the root of gratitude is “It’s all grace.” With self on the throne, we take our spouse’s efforts for granted; the self-emptied know that everything is God’s grace, coming to us through our spouse. Gratitude draws out gratitude, just as humility draws out humility, and the atmosphere of the home slowly changes.
lessons.jesus: Four thousand people were in the wilderness, and there were only seven loaves in hand. Jesus didn’t first complain that it was too little; “he took the seven loaves. Having given thanks, he broke them” (Mark 8:6), and gave them out to the crowd. The thanks came before the miracle, not after it. Jesus shows us that giving thanks for what looks small in front of us is where abundance begins.
lessons.pray: Gracious Father, thank you for caring for us every day through each other. We admit that we often take your grace for granted, and complaints come faster than thanks. Renew our eyes and our lips, so that we see each other’s efforts and say our thanks out loud. Fill our home with the sound of gratitude. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: A home is full of “invisible work”: taking out the trash, paying the bills, remembering the grandparents’ birthdays, restocking the toilet paper. When it gets done, no one notices; only when it’s forgotten does anyone pay attention. Over time, the one doing it starts to feel like air: present, but never seen. A simple “thank you” is like switching on a light, so those invisible efforts can finally be seen.

When Paul wrote to the church in Philippi, he began, “I thank my God whenever I remember you” (Philippians 1:3). His reason for thanks was specific: “for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now” (Philippians 1:5). This is a wonderful example: when we think of our spouse, let thanks come first, and let it be specific, remembering all the way from “the first day until now.”

“Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Colossians 3:17). Gratitude goes in two directions: we say it to God, and we say it to people. We can practice “Three Thanks a Day”: every night before bed, each of you names three small things you want to thank the other for that day. It may feel a little awkward at first, but if you keep it up, your eyes will be trained to see grace more readily, rather than only seeing what is lacking.
q: What “invisible work” does my spouse do at home that I rarely notice or thank him or her for?
Do I often keep my thanks inside, while letting my complaints come out easily?
talk: Take turns naming three small things you want to thank each other for today; the more specific, the better.
Which of the things you do at home would you most like to be noticed and thanked for?
acts: Tonight before bed, tell your spouse your “three thanks” for today
Formally thank your spouse for something he or she has done for a long time without anyone saying thanks
Thank God for one specific thing your spouse has done
lessons.noon: “I thank my God whenever I remember you” — Lord, right now as I think of my spouse, I thank you for him or her.

lessons.title: Speaking God’s Blessing
lessons.theme: To bless is to speak God’s good purposes into your spouse’s life

v: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’ You shall tell them,
‘The LORD bless you, and keep you.
The LORD make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.
The LORD lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.’
“So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them.”

lessons.still: Quietly imagine God lifting up his face toward you, looking at you with love. Let this sense of being blessed fill you. Then whisper to the Lord, “Lord, make me a blessing to my spouse today, too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Words of cursing define our spouse from a human point of view: “That’s just how you are.” Words of blessing see our spouse from God’s point of view: “God is going to do good things in you.” The focus shifts from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal. We are not our spouse’s judge; we are an outlet for God’s blessing.
lessons.jesus: Before Jesus ascended, his last act was to bless: “he lifted up his hands and blessed them. While he blessed them, he withdrew from them” (Luke 24:50–51). The last picture he left his disciples was not a rebuke but lifted hands. Jesus’ blessing still covers every home that follows him today.
lessons.pray: LORD who blesses, thank you for making your face shine on us and being gracious to us. Make our mouths mouths of blessing; let us no longer predict each other’s failures, but speak your good purposes. Bless our home, keep us, lift up your face toward us, and give us peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
teach: In the Bible, a blessing is not just a polite pleasantry; it speaks God’s good purposes into a person’s life. God told Aaron and his sons, “This is how you shall bless the children of Israel” (Numbers 6:23), and he himself taught them the words of the blessing: “The LORD bless you, and keep you” (Numbers 6:24). Words of blessing are words God himself designed and himself promised to fulfill.

This blessing has three layers. Blessing and keeping speak of provision for daily life. God making his face shine on us and being gracious speaks of closeness in relationship. God lifting up his face toward us and giving us peace speaks of rest for the soul. Finally God says, “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them” (Numbers 6:27). When we bless our spouse in the Lord’s name, it is God himself who pours out the blessing.

Husbands and wives can both bless each other. You might begin like this: before leaving in the morning, rest your hand lightly on your spouse’s shoulder and say, “May the Lord keep you safe in your going out and coming in today, and give you wisdom and joy.” At night before sleep, say, “May the Lord give you rest tonight.” A blessing takes less than ten seconds, yet it lets your spouse carry the confidence “I am blessed” into a whole day of pressure and challenges.
q: Do the words I say to my spouse sound more like a blessing, or more like predicting their failure?
Do I really believe that God wants to bless my spouse and our home?
talk: Bless each other with Numbers 6:24–26, putting your spouse’s name in place of “you.” How did it feel to be blessed?
What would you most like me to bless you with each day?
acts: Today, put your hand on your spouse’s shoulder and speak one sentence of blessing over him or her
Copy out Numbers 6:24–26 and post it by your front door
Bless your spouse silently in your heart three times today
lessons.noon: “The LORD bless you, and keep you” — Lord, right now bless my spouse and keep him or her.

lessons.title: Encourage One Another Every Day
lessons.theme: Words that build up need to become a daily habit

v: but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called “today”, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.

lessons.still: Look back over this week: tearing down and building up, affirmation, thanks, blessing. Quietly thank the Lord, because his word builds you up every day. Then ask him, “Lord, what word that builds up should I say to my spouse tomorrow?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Of the eight steps for changing your mindset, “repetition” is the one most easily neglected. Knowing the value of good words is “information”; starting to say them is “practice”; saying them every day is how they become part of who we are. Live from the heart by the Spirit; there is no need to push through on your own. Ask the Holy Spirit each day for one word to say, and he will gladly provide it.
lessons.jesus: The disciples were terrified in the storm, thinking they were seeing a ghost. “But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, ‘Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.’” (Matthew 14:27). He didn’t first rebuke their little faith; his very first words were words of comfort. In the Gospels, Jesus often tells people to “cheer up.” His encouragement always comes in time, and he is never stingy with it.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for building us up with your word every day. Help us turn words that build up into a daily habit in our home: while it is still called “today,” let us encourage one another and build each other up. Don’t let our hearts grow hard, and don’t let our spouse’s heart grow hard. May our home be a place where good words always live. Amen.
teach: A potted plant doesn’t thrive on one big watering a week; it needs a little water every day. Good words in a marriage are the same. Hebrews says, “exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). “Day by day” and “so long as it is called ‘today’” remind us that encouragement can’t wait, and can’t be saved only for anniversaries.

This verse also reveals a spiritual truth: without encouragement, hearts slowly harden. Many marriages don’t go cold all at once; after a long time without hearing a single good word, the heart hardens bit by bit. On the other hand, a good word every day is like loosening the soil of the heart daily. Proverbs says, “Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad” (Proverbs 12:25). Just one word can lift a heart that has been bent low.

You can build a small habit for your home: “one word that builds up, every day.” Before leaving in the morning or before bed at night, say one word of affirmation, thanks, or blessing to your spouse. You can also rotate the three: affirmation today, thanks tomorrow, blessing the day after. At first you will need reminders, but over time good words will become your home’s mother tongue. Friends and family who visit will hear the voice of Christ in a home like that.
q: This week, which kind of good word (affirmation, thanks, or blessing) was hardest for me to say? Why?
Has my heart grown hard from a long lack of encouragement? Am I willing to hand it to the Lord?
talk: Of everything I said to you this week, which words would you most like to keep?
At what time each day will we say our “one word that builds up”? Let’s set the time together. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down the first thing you will say tomorrow.)
acts: Set a daily time to say “one word that builds up”
Say the first one today, and note it on your phone
Invite your spouse to join you in going seven days in a row without a single sarcastic remark
lessons.noon: “a kind word makes it glad” — Lord, right now give me one good word to say to my spouse today.

34.title: Death and Life in the Power of the Tongue

mem.t: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

date.t: Take Back One Word, Plant a New One
s: Each of you quietly look back: in this marriage, is there something you once said that hurt the other? Choose one that is suitable to talk about gently tonight.
Take turns saying: “I once said… I know those words hurt you. I take them back, and I'm sorry.” The listener can respond: “Thank you. I'm willing to let it go.”
Then take turns saying one life-giving sentence to replace it: “What I really want to say to you is…”
Read Proverbs 18:21 together and pray as one: “Lord, let the tongues in our home bear the fruit of life.”

lessons.title: A Small Rudder, a Big Ship
lessons.theme: The tongue is small, yet it can set the course of a marriage

v: Indeed, we put bits into the horses’ mouths so that they may obey us, and we guide their whole body.
Behold, the ships also, though they are so big and are driven by fierce winds, are yet guided by a very small rudder, wherever the pilot desires.
So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity among our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

lessons.still: Be still and notice your tongue in your mouth—how small it is. Say to the Lord: “Lord, this little part of me can bring life to my home today, or it can bring death. I place it in your hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The tongue is hard to tame because it follows the heart; whoever sits on the throne of the heart is the one the tongue speaks for. With self on the throne, the tongue defends, attacks, and retaliates for self; when we let Jesus reign, the tongue becomes a vessel of life-giving words. The best way to rein in my tongue is first to let Jesus rule my heart.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life” (John 6:63). With a single word he raised the dead, calmed the storm, and forgave sinners. Jesus' words carry authority, yet he always uses them to bring life. Following him means letting our limited tongues become outlets for his life-giving words, too.
lessons.pray: Lord, your words are spirit and life. We confess that our tongues have often been like fire, hurting the people closest to us. Cleanse our hearts and govern our mouths. May our tongues no longer kindle anger, but become a tree of life, bearing the fruit of peace and joy. Amen.
teach: James paints three pictures: a bit can steer a horse's whole body; even huge ships “are yet guided by a very small rudder” (James 3:4); and “See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!” (James 3:5). All three make the same point: small things have big effects. The tongue is a small part of the body, yet it often decides where a home is heading—toward a safe harbor, or onto the rocks.

Proverbs says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit” (Proverbs 18:21). The Hebrew literally says “in the hand of the tongue”: it is as if the tongue had a hand, holding life and death in its grip. The second half reminds us that words bear fruit, and the speaker has to eat it too. People who keep speaking harshly end up living in a harsh home; people who keep speaking kindly end up living in a kind one.

James puts it bluntly: “the tongue is a fire” (James 3:6). Looking back, many couples find that their deepest wound came not from a particular event but from a particular sentence: “I should never have married you,” “You're exactly like your father.” The incident is long over, but those words keep burning in the heart. This week we will take the power of words seriously and learn to hand the rudder of our tongue to the Holy Spirit.
q: Looking back on this marriage, is there something I said that burned my spouse like fire?
What kind of fruit are my everyday words producing in our home?
talk: Is there something kind I once said that you still remember? How did it affect you?
If the words in our home were the rudder of a ship, where do you think the ship is heading right now?
acts: Before speaking, ask: What fruit will these words bear?
Say one life-giving sentence to your spouse
If you remember a harsh thing you once said, find a chance to apologize today
lessons.noon: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” — Lord, right now, let my tongue bring life.

lessons.title: A Knife with a Smile: Sarcasm and Mockery
lessons.theme: “Just kidding” can still cut deep

v: Like a madman who shoots torches, arrows, and death,
is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, “Am I not joking?”
There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.

lessons.still: Pause and recall something you often say that you consider “just a joke.” If your spouse said it to you, how would you feel inside? Bring that feeling before the Lord and ask him for a gentle heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Sarcasm is a hidden form of pride—putting the other person down to lift myself up, or wrapping my discontent in a joke. A humble person doesn't need to step on others to look good. Let people be people, and let God be God: my spouse is not a target for my jokes, but a fellow heir with me of the grace of life.
lessons.jesus: The soldiers put a crown of thorns on Jesus, knelt before him and mocked him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” (Matthew 27:29). It was mockery at its most humiliating. Jesus did not answer with sarcasm or retaliate with words. He bore it in silence, in order to save the very people who mocked him. He knows the pain of being ridiculed, and he is willing to heal wounds like ours.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we sometimes wrap a blade in a joke and hurt each other without even realizing it. Forgive our pride and take the barbs out of our words. Make our tongues medicine that heals, so that the laughter in our home is two people laughing together, not one laughing while the other weeps inside. Amen.
teach: Sarcasm is like a knife coated in sugar: a smile on the outside, a sharp blade underneath. “Wow, home on time today? Must be a blue moon!” “Your cooking is really… ‘special.’” The speaker thinks it's funny and others laugh, but the one on the receiving end feels a sting—and can't even get upset, because getting upset means being told, “You can't take a joke.”

Proverbs captures this vividly: “Like a madman who shoots torches, arrows, and death, is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, ‘Am I not joking?’” (Proverbs 26:18–19). Hurling a torch and then saying “just kidding” doesn't make the damage any smaller. Proverbs also says, “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals” (Proverbs 12:18). The same tongue can be a sword, or it can be medicine.

Sarcasm is often a complaint we don't dare to say directly. Instead of “Must be a blue moon,” say honestly: “I'm really happy you came home early today, because I've been wishing for more time with you.” Take out the barb and keep the heart. If you notice you've just said something cutting, repair it right away: “Sorry, that wasn't funny. I take it back.”
q: Which of my “jokes” is really a way of venting my frustration with my spouse?
When my spouse mocks me, what do I really feel inside? How do I usually react?
talk: Is there a kind of joke you wish I would stop making? Please tell me gently—I'll listen carefully.
Can we agree to make only jokes that both of us can laugh at? Where do you think the line is?
acts: Today, don't make a single cutting joke
If you slip, say right away: “Sorry, that wasn't funny.”
Turn one sarcastic remark into an honest word from the heart
lessons.noon: “the tongue of the wise heals” — Lord, right now, make my words a source of healing, not a blade.

lessons.title: The Damage Done by Comparison and Threats
lessons.theme: Comparison steals gratitude; threats destroy security

v: For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.

lessons.still: Be still and consider: Have I compared my spouse with others, in my heart or out loud? Have I, in a moment of anger, said things that made my spouse afraid? No need to rush into self-blame—just honestly hand it to the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Comparison fixes our eyes on other people; threats try to force change through power. Both are self on the throne: I want to be in charge. When my focus returns to Jesus, I don't need to compare, because he has already accepted me; nor do I need to control anyone with fear, because he alone is Lord of this home.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told a parable about vineyard workers. Those hired early saw the latecomers receive the same wage and began to grumble. The landowner said, “Is your eye evil, because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15). Comparison blinds us to the grace already in our hands. Through this parable Jesus pulls our eyes away from others and back to the generosity of God.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we often measure our spouse's weaknesses against other people's strengths, and that we have spoken in anger in ways that made each other afraid. Forgive us. Help us examine only ourselves and not judge each other. May our home be a safe place, with no fear, only love. And if anyone is living with verbal abuse right now, protect them and lead them to help. Amen.
teach: “Look how thoughtful her husband is.” “My coworker's wife would never do that.” Words of comparison are like a ruler, and what they measure is always the other person's shortfall. Paul says that those “measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:12), and reminds us, “let each man examine his own work” (Galatians 6:4). God doesn't ask us to measure our spouse against others, but to examine ourselves first. Besides, we usually compare someone else's best side with our spouse's most ordinary days.

Another kind of word does even more damage: threats. “Do that again and I'm leaving!” “Let's just get divorced!” It may be said only in anger, but it punches a hole in the foundation of the marriage, and your spouse starts to wonder: Could this home fall apart at any moment? People who live in fear don't love more; they only become more guarded. Threats don't bring real change. They bring fear, people-pleasing, or counterattack—but never true intimacy.

We need to be clear: when a husband or wife occasionally says the wrong thing, it calls for repentance and repair. But if one spouse persistently uses words to humiliate, intimidate, or control the other—for example, threatening to hurt them, restricting their access to money, or forbidding them to see other people—that is abuse and control, not an ordinary quarrel, and it is certainly not something to simply “endure.” Forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. Safety comes first: please seek help as soon as possible from a pastor you trust and from professional services.
q: Who do I most often compare my spouse with? What fruit does this comparison produce in my heart?
Have I ever, in anger, talked about “leaving” or made threats? How do I want to respond to God and to my spouse about this?
talk: When do you most feel compared by me? Please tell me gently so I can understand you better.
Can we promise each other together: no matter how bad the fight, we will never threaten “divorce” or “leaving”?
acts: Replace one comparison with a word of thanks to your spouse
Tell your spouse: “No matter how hard things get, I will never threaten you with leaving.”
If you are living under intimidation or control, contact a pastor you trust today
lessons.noon: “let each man examine his own work” — Lord, right now I lay down comparison and examine myself first.

lessons.title: A Soft Tongue Breaks the Bone
lessons.theme: Gentle words are stronger than loud ones

v: By patience a ruler is persuaded. A soft tongue breaks the bone.
They replied, “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever.”
The king answered the people roughly, and abandoned the counsel of the old men which they had given him,

and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.”

lessons.still: Be still. Slow your breathing and relax your shoulders. Imagine Jesus calling your name in a gentle voice. Let that voice linger in your heart for a while, then say to the Lord: “Lord, please put your gentleness into my voice.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Raising our voice is often an attempt to overpower the other person; speaking gently means trusting that God is stronger than I am. Pride against pride only makes voices louder; humility draws out humility, and gentleness draws out gentleness. When I let Jesus reign, I don't need volume to win respect.
lessons.jesus: People told Jesus to his face that he was a Samaritan and had a demon. Jesus didn't raise his voice or hurl insults back. He calmly said, “I don't have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me” (John 8:49). He spoke the truth without being provoked. Real strength doesn't need to prove itself by being loud.
lessons.pray: Gentle and humble Lord, thank you for never shouting at us. We confess that we often try to beat each other with volume and harsh words. Holy Spirit, grow the fruit of gentleness in us, so that we answer each other with good words, so that anger in our home subsides, and so that our hardened hearts melt in your gentleness. Amen.
teach: Many people think the louder you are, the stronger you are—and that in a fight, the fiercer you get, the more likely you are to win. But Proverbs says something remarkable: “A soft tongue breaks the bone” (Proverbs 25:15). Bone is the hardest part of the body, a picture of the most stubborn resistance in the human heart. What breaks it is not shouting, but softness. Just as dripping water wears away stone, steady gentleness softens a heart more than a sudden burst of force.

When Rehoboam first became king, the people asked him to lighten their burden. The elders advised him: “If you will be a servant to this people today, and will serve them, and answer them with good words, then they will be your servants forever” (1 Kings 12:7). But he listened to the young men instead: “The king answered the people roughly” (1 Kings 12:13). As a result, the kingdom split in two. One harsh answer tore a nation apart; at home, it can tear a marriage apart.

Gentleness is not weakness, nor is it avoiding the truth. It is speaking the truth in a way governed by the Holy Spirit. Here is a practical way to practice: lower your volume, slow your pace, and respond first to the other person's feelings. For example, if your spouse says, “You don't care about me at all!” don't answer, “How don't I care?” Instead say, “I can hear that you're really hurting. I'd like to hear more.” Gentleness is a fruit of the Spirit, not just a personality trait; even the most short-tempered person can learn it in the Spirit.
q: In a conflict, how do my volume and tone usually change?
Do I treat “loud” as if it meant “right”? What kind of heart lies behind that?
talk: When my voice gets louder, what do you feel inside? What would you like me to do?
Can we agree on a small hand signal to remind each other to “lower the volume”? Let's come up with one together right now.
acts: When you speak today, deliberately lower your volume and slow down
Agree with your spouse on a “lower the volume” hand signal
When your spouse is upset, first respond: “I can hear that you're really hurting.”
lessons.noon: “A soft tongue breaks the bone” — Lord, right now, let my voice carry your gentleness.

lessons.title: Bless Instead of Curse
lessons.theme: When words wound us, choose to respond with blessing

v: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?
Can a fig tree, my brothers, yield olives, or a vine figs? Thus no spring yields both salt water and fresh water.
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.

lessons.still: Look back on this week: the power of the tongue, the knife with a smile, comparison and threats, the soft tongue. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, in our home, which blessing do you want me to speak in place of which curse?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Returning insult for insult is pride against pride—both sides lose. Answering insult with blessing is humility drawing out humility—both sides win. This doesn't come from willpower but from the cross: Jesus has already borne my sin, so I can hand others' offenses over to him instead of taking revenge myself.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus knew Judas would betray him, yet “when he had dipped the piece of bread, he gave it to Judas” (John 13:26). He did not expose or shame him in front of the others. On the cross he went further and asked the Father to forgive those who crucified him. Jesus is our example, and he is also the source of strength that lets us answer hurt with blessing.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, when you were insulted you did not retaliate, but asked for grace for others. We confess that we often return insult for insult and let hurt be passed along in our home. Give us new hearts, so that when we are wounded we can pause, hand the offense to you, and bless instead of curse. May our home inherit the blessing you have promised. Amen.
teach: When our spouse's words wound us, the most natural reaction is to strike back—more precisely, more painfully.
