So it goes, one remark after another, like two people throwing stones at each other until both are hurt. But Jesus says: “bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you” (Luke 6:28). He is not asking us to pretend it doesn't hurt, but, while it hurts, to choose not to let the evil travel any further.

James says: “Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so” (James 3:10). On Sunday we worship God with our lips, then go home and use the same mouth to tear into our spouse. Our spouse is one of the “men who are made in the image of God” (James 3:9); to curse them is to treat God's image with contempt. James goes on to ask: “Does a spring send out from the same opening fresh and bitter water?” (James 3:11)

Responding with blessing is not weakness; it is a greater strength. Here is a concrete way to do it: when you're hurt, pause first and pray silently, “Lord, bless him (or her)”; once your emotions settle, say honestly, “What you just said really hurt me. I don't want to answer you the same way. Can we talk this through?” That way you speak the truth without letting the evil keep circling. This is overcoming evil with good.
q: When my spouse's words wound me, what words do I most often use to strike back?
Is there a “curse” I need to stop saying, such as “You'll never amount to anything”?
talk: Think back to a conversation where we hurt each other. If we could do it over, how would you want each of us to speak?
Speak a word of blessing over each other to close this week. (If your spouse can't join you for now, write down a sentence of blessing you want to give them.)
acts: When offended, first say in your heart: “Lord, bless them.”
Before bed, speak a blessing over your spouse
Write down one cursing phrase you've decided never to say again, confess it to the Lord, then tear it up
lessons.noon: “bless those who curse you” — Lord, right now I choose to answer with blessing, not harsh words.

35.title: Deep Waters of the Heart: Saying What We Really Need

mem.t: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.

date.t: Drawing Up the Waters of the Heart Together
s: Set aside an uninterrupted time for a walk or a cup of tea, with your phones on silent.
Take turns answering three questions: “What has made you happiest lately?” “What has been weighing on you most lately?” “In this season, what do you need from me most?”
The listener gives no advice and responds with just one sentence: “I hear you saying… Is that right?”
Finally, hold hands and read Proverbs 20:5 together, then pray for the needs each of you has shared.

lessons.title: The Heart Is Like Deep Water
lessons.theme: Beneath our words lies a deeper heart

v: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.
The heart knows its own bitterness and joy; he will not share these with a stranger.

lessons.still: Be still and imagine yourself standing at the edge of a very deep well. You look down and cannot see the bottom. Your heart is like that. Say to the Lord: “Lord, only you fully know the depths of my heart. Please help me see my true heart today.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Those who live from the head hear only the surface words and rush to argue or fix; those who live from the heart see the heart through the words. The issues of life flow from the heart, and the problems in a marriage are often problems of the heart. Only as the Holy Spirit leads us into each other's depths can our relationship move from surface peace to true oneness.
lessons.jesus: Jesus asked a man who had lain by the pool for years, “Do you want to be made well?” (John 5:6). The man didn't answer yes or no. Instead he said, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up” (John 5:7). An answer that missed the question revealed the loneliness in the deep water: “I have no one.” Jesus heard that heart, and healed him himself.
lessons.pray: Lord who searches hearts, you know us completely and love us completely. Help us see the deep waters in our own hearts, so that we no longer attack each other with surface words. Give us hearts of understanding to draw out each other's hearts patiently and gently, so that our marriage moves from the surface into the depths. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Only a small part of an iceberg shows above the water; most of it is hidden below. The words between husband and wife are like that. On the surface it's “You forgot to take out the trash again,” but underneath it may be “I feel like I'm the only one holding this home together.” On the surface it's “Why are you always on your phone?” but underneath it may be “I'm so lonely; I want you to see me.” If we only deal with the words above the waterline, we will never reach the real issue.

Proverbs says, “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out” (Proverbs 20:5). “Counsel” here means the thoughts and motives hidden deep in the heart. The human heart is like a deep well: the water is there, but it has to be drawn up slowly with a rope and bucket—you can't throw stones into it. Blaming, rushing, and hurrying to analyze are all like throwing stones down the well; patience, curiosity, and gentleness are the rope.

Elsewhere Proverbs says, “The heart knows its own bitterness and joy; he will not share these with a stranger” (Proverbs 14:10). Every heart has parts others can't easily know—even the spouse closest to us. So don't assume, “I already know what you're thinking.” This week we will learn two things: first to see and name the deep waters in our own heart, and then to gently draw out the heart of our spouse.
q: Which recent complaint I made to my spouse was hiding some feeling beneath the surface?
Do I often assume “I already know what my spouse is thinking” and stop being curious?
talk: Has there been something lately where what you said and what you really felt inside didn't quite match? Would you be willing to talk about it?
When do you feel I'm best at “drawing out” your heart? When does it feel most like I'm throwing stones?
acts: When your spouse complains, ask yourself: What's the feeling underneath?
Write down something recent that bothered you but you never said
Ask your spouse: “Is anything weighing on your heart today?”
lessons.noon: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water” — Lord, right now help me see the heart beneath my spouse's words.

lessons.title: State the Need, Not the Blame
lessons.theme: Trade “You don't care” for “I need”

v: I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.
If you treat me this way, please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight; and don’t let me see my wretchedness.”

The LORD said to Moses, “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and officers over them; and bring them to the Tent of Meeting, that they may stand there with you.

I will come down and talk with you there. I will take of the Spirit which is on you, and will put it on them; and they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you don’t bear it yourself alone.

lessons.still: Be still and think of the last complaint you made to your spouse. Beneath it, what did you really need? Help, rest, companionship, or to be seen? Gently tell the Lord: “Lord, what I really need is…”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life turns needs into demands: “You should have known!” The self-emptied life names the need honestly and leaves the outcome to God. My spouse is not my savior and cannot meet all my needs; only God can meet the deepest ones. In the end, it was God himself who provided people to share the load Moses couldn't carry.
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus said, “I am thirsty!” (John 19:28). It was a very short sentence, yet in it the Son of God openly named a need of his body. He didn't blame anyone for not looking after him; he simply said it. Jesus shows us that admitting a need is not shameful—it is part of being truly human, and an act of trust in others.
lessons.pray: Lord, like Moses we often speak harshly under heavy burdens, wrapping our exhaustion and longings in blame. Help us state our needs honestly and respond gently to each other's needs. And remind us that only you can meet our deepest needs. Fill us with yourself first, so that we can love each other. Amen.
teach: Moses led the people through the wilderness while they complained day after day. At last he broke down and said harsh words to God: “If you treat me this way, please kill me right now” (Numbers 11:15). Those words were full of blame and despair. But underneath them was his truest cry: “I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me” (Numbers 11:14). It was the cry of a heart exhausted to the limit and longing for someone to share the load.

God's response is remarkable. He was not provoked by Moses' harsh words; he heard the need beneath them. He told Moses to gather seventy elders: “they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you don't bear it yourself alone” (Numbers 11:17). Many couples' conversations get stuck because we wrap our needs in blame. The other person hears only the blame, not the need, and gets defensive—so the need goes even more unmet.

We can practice translating blame into need with this full sentence pattern: “When…, I feel…, because I need… Would you be willing to…?” For example: “When I'm cleaning up alone until late at night, I feel exhausted and a bit lonely, because I need someone to share the load and keep me company. Would you be willing to clean up with me for fifteen minutes tonight?” A specific request shows your spouse how to love you.
q: What blaming words do I most often use to wrap up my own needs?
Do I expect my spouse to meet some needs that only God can meet?
talk: Each of you name one recent need using “When… I feel… because I need… Would you be willing to…?”
After hearing your spouse's need, tell them: “Here's a specific way I'm willing to respond…”
acts: Change one complaint into “I need… Would you be willing to…?”
Respond in a specific way to one need your spouse has expressed
Spend five minutes sitting quietly at the Lord's feet and tell him your needs first
lessons.noon: “they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you don't bear it yourself alone” — Lord, right now I hand you first the burden I cannot carry.

lessons.title: First Pour Out Your Heart Before God
lessons.theme: Knowing our own heart begins with telling God the truth

v: Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us. Selah.
I cry with my voice to the LORD. With my voice, I ask the LORD for mercy.
I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles.

lessons.still: Find a quiet corner. You don't need polished words. Speak to the Lord as you would to your most trusted friend: “Lord, right now I feel…” Let it flow naturally. He understands it all.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God → self → others → things. Only when we are aligned with God can we truly know ourselves, and only when we know ourselves can we truly connect with our spouse. If we skip God and dump our emotions straight onto our spouse, it often turns into hurt; if we pour them out before God first, what our spouse hears is honesty that has passed through prayer.
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). It was the prayer of Psalm 22, and the most honest cry there is. Jesus did not hide his pain; he brought it before his Father. He shows us that telling God what is truly in our hearts is itself an expression of faith.
lessons.pray: Our refuge, thank you for being willing to hear us pour out our hearts. We often face each other with chaotic emotions and end up hurting each other. Teach us to come to you first and pour out our hearts, so that you can untangle, comfort, and heal; then let us speak the truth to each other with calm hearts. Amen.
teach: Many people can't explain their feelings to their spouse because they don't even know what's going on inside themselves. They only know they're irritated or weighed down, but can't say whether it's disappointment, fear, or feeling wronged. It's like a tangled ball of yarn: you have to loosen it slowly before you can hand it to someone else. When our thoughts aren't sorted out, what comes out of our mouths is often heavier than what we meant, or misses the point entirely. And the best place to sort out our hearts is before God.

The psalmist says, “Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). Pouring out your heart is like turning a full bottle upside down and emptying it to the last drop. David, in the cave, says, “I pour out my complaint before him. I tell him my troubles” (Psalm 142:2). The Psalms hold joy, but also tears, anger, and questions—and God receives them all.

This gives us a practical order: tell God first, then tell your spouse. Before God you can pour out your most intense, most chaotic emotions without fear of hurting anyone. Once you've poured them out, your heart is clearer and calmer, and you can go to your spouse with a heart that has been sorted out. Try keeping a “heart journal”: What am I feeling today? Why? What do I need? What am I handing over to God?
q: If I used three words to describe what I feel inside right now, what would they be?
What emotions have I never honestly expressed before God?
talk: When your heart is in turmoil, do you need me to give you some space, or to stay close to you?
Let's practice together: each of us prays quietly for five minutes first, then shares one thing that's on our heart today.
acts: Today, spend five minutes telling God how you truly feel
Write today's heart journal: feelings, reasons, needs
Pray before discussing important matters with your spouse
lessons.noon: “Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us.” — Lord, right now I pour out everything in my heart before you.

lessons.title: Good Questions Are the Rope That Draws Water
lessons.theme: With curiosity and gentleness, invite your spouse to share their heart

v: He came to a cave there, and camped there; and behold, the LORD’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
After the earthquake a fire passed; but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

lessons.still: Be still and imagine God gently asking you, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). Put your own name in place of Elijah's and answer him honestly. Then ask the Lord to give you the same gentle curiosity as you reach out to your spouse's heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: With self on the throne, we listen to our spouse while waiting for our turn to talk; the self-emptied heart sets aside its own agenda and enters fully into the other person's world. People matter more than tasks: more important than solving the problem is letting your spouse know, “You matter to me.”
lessons.jesus: When two men began following Jesus, he turned around and asked them, “What are you looking for?” (John 1:38). In John's Gospel, these are the first words Jesus speaks. He didn't rush to introduce himself or teach; first he invited them to voice the longing of their hearts. A good question is often the beginning of a deep friendship.
lessons.pray: Loving Lord, thank you that even when we hide in our caves, you still ask after us gently and patiently hear our disappointments and questions. Give us that same heart: to let go of our habit of rushing to speak, and to draw out the deep waters of each other's hearts with curiosity and gentleness. Make our home a place where it is safe to speak from the heart. Amen.
teach: After his great victory on Mount Carmel, Elijah fled into the wilderness because of Jezebel's threat. Worn out, he asked to die and hid in a cave. God knew everything, yet he first asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (1 Kings 19:9). Elijah poured out all his bitterness: “I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away” (1 Kings 19:10). God didn't interrupt or rush to correct him; he let him finish.

Then God was not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12), and he asked the same question a second time. A good question is like the rope that draws water; sometimes you have to ask twice before the water comes up. Closed questions only get you “Fine.” Open questions unlock the heart: “What was the most draining moment of your day?” “What were you most worried about then?” Then add: “What else? Can you tell me more?”

As you draw water, avoid three kinds of stones: rushing to give advice (“Just do it this way”), rushing to compare (“I'm even more tired than you”), and rushing to defend yourself (“I didn't mean to”). Practice a simple response: “I hear you saying… Is that right?” And finally ask, “How can I be with you in this?” Let your spouse decide whether what they need is advice, help, or simply your company.
q: Are the questions I usually ask my spouse open, or can they only be answered “good” or “not good”?
When my spouse shares, which “stone” do I throw most often: advice, comparison, or defensiveness?
talk: Take turns asking each other: “This week, what has been most on your heart?” After listening, ask once more: “What else?”
Finally, ask each other: “How can I be with you in this?” and listen carefully to the answer.
acts: Ask your spouse one open question today, and listen all the way to the end
When your spouse finishes, ask one more time: “What else?”
Ask your spouse today: “How can I be with you in this?”
lessons.noon: “After the fire, there was a still small voice.” — Lord, right now speak to me in your still small voice.

lessons.title: Heart Talk: A Weekly Time in the Deep Waters
lessons.theme: In the safety of acceptance, keep opening your hearts to each other

v: Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart; so does earnest counsel from a man’s friend.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, arose and went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God.
He said to him, “Don’t be afraid, for the hand of Saul my father won’t find you; and you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you; and Saul my father knows that also.”

lessons.still: Look back on this week: the deep waters of the heart, stating needs, pouring out our hearts to God, drawing each other out. Quietly thank the Lord that he has accepted the real you. Ask him to make your home a safe place for real conversation, too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the eight steps of changing your mindset, the steps “practice, review, adjust, repeat” need a steady rhythm. One deep conversation won't change a marriage; ongoing heart-to-heart sharing changes lives, and then relationships. Life first, then relationships: when each of us comes to Christ first and then comes to the other, our conversations will grow deeper and deeper.
lessons.jesus: In everyone's eyes Matthew was a tax collector, yet Jesus said to him, “Follow me” (Matthew 9:9), and then sat down to eat with many tax collectors and sinners. Jesus offered acceptance first, and only then did people dare to open their hearts. Acceptance is not approving of everything; it is giving people a sense of safety so they are willing to bring out their true selves.
lessons.pray: Lord who accepts us, thank you for accepting us even when we were most unlovable. Make our home a safe place where we dare to share the deep waters of our hearts. Help us keep our weekly heart talk, strengthening each other and leaning on you together, so that our marriage grows ever deeper and the glory goes to you. Amen.
teach: A well needs water drawn from it regularly to stay fresh and sweet; left unused, it silts up. Opening our hearts to each other as husband and wife is the same: it needs a regular time, not just when something goes wrong. Proverbs says, “Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart; so does earnest counsel from a man's friend” (Proverbs 27:9). Husband and wife are the closest of friends, and honest conversation between them should be sweet, not frightening.

Try setting up a weekly “heart talk” of about twenty minutes: 1. Begin with a short prayer together, asking for the Holy Spirit's presence. 2. The speaker shares one thing using “When… I feel… because I need… Would you be willing to…?” 3. The listener reflects back: “I hear you saying… Is that right?” and then asks, “What else?” 4. Switch roles. 5. Pray for each other's needs.

Add a few safety agreements: no dredging up the past, no interrupting, no passing judgment during the conversation, and never using what was shared in confidence as a weapon in a fight. When David was in his darkest days, Jonathan “went to David into the woods, and strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16). Heart talk is not about winning an argument; like Jonathan, it is about strengthening each other's hand in God. Keep it up, and the two of you will know each other more and more, and draw closer and closer to Christ.
q: Does my spouse feel safe sharing their heart with me? What have I done that makes them feel safe or unsafe?
This week, what new insight has God given me into my own heart?
talk: When each week will we have our “heart talk”? Decide on a time and place together.
Try it today: using the five steps in this lesson, each share one thing on your heart. (If your spouse can't join you for now, write down what you want to say and give it to the Lord first.)
acts: Set a weekly “heart talk” time with your spouse
Write the five steps on a card and keep it where you talk
Tell your spouse: “What you share with me from your heart, I will keep safe.”
lessons.noon: “so does earnest counsel from a man's friend” — Lord, right now make me a safe place for my spouse.

mem.t: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?

date.t: Digging Treasure Out of an Argument
s: Together, choose a small friction that has come up often lately but isn't too serious—such as dividing chores, scheduling time, or how you spend money.
Each of you quietly write down: “In this matter, what do I really want?” Then write: “Has this want become a ‘must-have’?”
Take turns sharing what you wrote. Talk only about yourself and don't analyze your spouse; the listener only says: “Thank you for helping me understand.”
Finally, pray together: “Lord, thank you for using this to help us see ourselves. Make us more like you.”

lessons.title: The Source of Conflict
lessons.theme: The root of conflict lies not in my spouse's faults but in the desires of my own heart

v: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

lessons.still: Be still and recall your most recent conflict with your spouse. Don't think yet about what they said or did. Just honestly ask the Lord: “Lord, what was I really fighting for in my heart back then?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The root of the problem is the self-ruled life: making myself the center, wanting to be lord and king. “Pride only breeds quarrels” (Proverbs 13:10); two people who both want to be king will inevitably go to war. Conflict is not just a lack of communication skills; it is a question of who sits on the throne of the heart. When we let Jesus reign, our selfish desires lose their throne.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught his disciples that what defiles us is not what goes in from outside, but that “from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts” (Mark 7:21). He added, “All these evil things come from within and defile the man” (Mark 7:23). Jesus turns our eyes from outward circumstances to the inner heart. It is the same when we look at conflict in marriage.
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that our quarrels often come not because the other person is so bad, but because the desires in our own hearts are so strong. Shine your light into our hearts so we can see what we are really fighting for. Take the throne of our hearts, so that we no longer ask with wrong motives but seek you alone. Amen.
teach: When there's a leak at home and the floor gets wet, we can mop and mop, only to find it wet again the next day; the problem is truly solved only when we find the broken pipe inside the wall. Marital conflict is the same. We often deal with the “wet floor”: who didn't do the dishes, who spoke too loudly. But James goes straight to the pipe: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don't they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1)

James's answer is surprising: the source of conflict is not outside us but inside. The word translated “pleasures” carries the sense of enjoyment and wanting, and what we want is not necessarily bad in itself: wanting rest, wanting respect, wanting to do things our own way. But when these “wants” go to war in our hearts and we must have them at any cost, we go to war with whoever stands in the way—and the person most often standing in the way is the spouse closest to us.

James also points to the way out: “You don't have, because you don't ask. You ask, and don't receive, because you ask with wrong motives” (James 4:2–3). Often we don't bring the wants of our hearts to God; we demand them straight from our spouse. Even when we pray, we only ask God to change our spouse so that we can get what we want. The first step in facing conflict is not to ask, “Where did they go wrong?” but, “What do I want in my heart?”
q: Thinking back to our most recent conflict, what did I really want in my heart?
Do I often ask God to change my spouse, yet rarely ask him to change my heart?
talk: In our most recent conflict, what do you think you were “fighting for”? Please speak only about your own part.
What kind of conflict comes up most often in our home? What shared “want” might lie behind it?
acts: When something upsets you, first ask: “What do I want in my heart?”
Bring one of your heart's “wants” before God and ask him first
Confess to God your own part in a recent conflict
lessons.noon: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” — Lord, right now help me see the selfish desires in my own heart.

lessons.title: From “Want” to “Must Have”
lessons.theme: Once a good desire takes the throne, it becomes an idol

v: But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.
Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.
“Son of man, these men have taken their idols into their heart, and put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face. Should I be inquired of at all by them?

lessons.still: Pause and consider: Is there something lately that, if my spouse doesn't do it my way, makes me really angry? Place it before the Lord and ask: “Lord, does this sit higher than you in my heart?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. When a task, a thing, or an idea becomes a “must-have,” I will hurt people for the sake of tasks and damage relationships for the sake of things. Repentance means giving the throne back to Jesus, letting my desires return to their rightful place, and letting God be God.
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, Jesus also had a real desire. He prayed, “Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Mark 14:36). Jesus shows us that having a desire is not a sin, nor is saying it honestly; when we place our desires under the Father's will, they won't turn into “must-haves.”
lessons.pray: Lord, we confess that we often put good desires on your throne, and judge and hurt each other because of them. Forgive us, and tear down the idols in our hearts. We want to give the throne back to you, let our desires return to their rightful place, and learn to serve one another in you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: James describes the growth of desire like a life cycle: “Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:15). In marriage the process often goes like this: first a “want,” such as wanting a good rest on the weekend; then it becomes a “must”: I have to rest; then it becomes “judgment”: You won't let me rest—you're so selfish; and finally “punishment”: the silent treatment, complaining, dredging up the past.

The “want” itself is often not bad. Wanting rest, wanting respect, wanting a tidy home are all good desires. The problem is their place. When a good thing takes the seat only God should occupy, it becomes an idol. God said to Ezekiel: “these men have taken their idols into their heart” (Ezekiel 14:3). An idol is not only a statue in a temple; it can also be a desire in our heart that we simply must have.

How can we tell that a desire has become an idol? Ask yourself: When I don't get it, do I judge or punish my spouse? Would I rather damage the relationship than give it up? One simple practice is to change a sentence: from “I have to have…” to “I would really love…, but I'm handing it to God.” The desire is still there, but God is back on the throne, and your spouse goes from enemy back to companion.
q: In our marriage, which of my “wants” has become a “must-have”?
When this desire isn't met, how do I usually judge or punish my spouse?
talk: Each of you say one sentence: “I would really love…, but I'm willing to hand it to God.”
Is there something you feel I'm insisting on as a “must-have”? Please tell me gently.
acts: Change “I have to have…” into “I would really love…, but I hand it to God”
Notice any judging thoughts toward your spouse today and confess them to the Lord
Let go of one small insistence and choose to go with your spouse's idea
lessons.noon: “each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed” — Lord, right now I give the throne of my heart back to you.

lessons.title: Examine Yourself First
lessons.theme: In conflict, let God shine his light on your own heart first

v: The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?
“I, the LORD, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.”
For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged.

lessons.still: Be still and open your heart to God, like drawing back the curtains to let sunlight into a room. Slowly pray: “Lord, shine your light into my heart and show me who I was in this conflict.” Don't rush to find answers; just let his light come in.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Moving from looking at others to looking at myself is the turning point from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life. The self-ruled person says, “If you hadn't done that, I wouldn't have done this.” The self-emptied person says, “Whatever you do, I'll deal with my part first.” Change begins with me; humility draws out humility, and often it is when one person bows first that both overcome together.
lessons.jesus: Some people told Jesus about Galileans whom Pilate had killed. Jesus asked in return, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered such things?” (Luke 13:2). Then he said, “unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way” (Luke 13:3). Jesus turned their gaze from discussing others back to their own repentance.
lessons.pray: God who searches the heart, shine your light into our hearts. We often look at our spouse through a magnifying glass, yet can't see ourselves clearly. Give us the courage to discern ourselves first and own our part, without shifting blame or making excuses. As we bow before you first, make us humble before each other too. Lead us to walk in your light. Amen.
teach: We often look at other people's faults through a magnifying glass, and at our own through frosted glass. In an argument we can clearly list ten problems with our spouse, yet struggle to name one of our own. The prophet Jeremiah says: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Even we ourselves cannot easily see our own hearts clearly.

God says: “I, the LORD, search the mind. I try the heart” (Jeremiah 17:10). Since only God can truly know the heart, the best thing we can do is ask him to shine his light on it. Paul says: “For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn't be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31). Notice whom we are to discern: ourselves, before anyone else—not our spouse. In a conflict, the hardest and most powerful prayer is to ask God to shine his light on me first.

After a conflict, you can examine yourself with three questions: 1. In this matter, what did I want in my heart? 2. What did I say or do that made things worse? 3. For which part do I need to apologize to my spouse? Talk only about your own part. Even if it's only ten percent, own that ten percent first. When one person starts looking at themselves, the other's defenses often come down too.
q: In our most recent conflict, what is “my part” that I need to own?
Do I often say or think, “If you hadn't done that, I wouldn't have done this”?
talk: Each of you say: “In our most recent conflict, where I fell short was…” Talk only about yourself, not your spouse. (If your spouse can't join you for now, write it in a notebook and give it to the Lord.)
When I own my part first, how does that make you feel?
acts: Pray one sentence: “Lord, shine your light on me first.”
Write down your own part in a recent conflict
Say to your spouse: “In that situation, I was wrong too.”
lessons.noon: “if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn't be judged” — Lord, right now shine your light on me first, not on my spouse.

lessons.title: Even Arguments Need Rules
lessons.theme: Healthy conflict has boundaries; violence and control are not conflict

v: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out.
It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling.

lessons.still: Be still and think about what your arguments look like. Are there words or actions you have deeply regretted afterward? Ask the Lord for wisdom: “Lord, teach us to respect each other even when we argue.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rules are not there to restrict love but to protect it. The self-ruled person argues to win, so no words are off limits; the self-emptied person, even when angry, remembers that their spouse is someone God loves. Don't hurt people for the sake of issues: we can argue about issues, but we must not attack the person.
lessons.jesus: Once, when the crowd picked up stones to throw at Jesus, Scripture says, “Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8:59). Jesus didn't stay in danger to prove anything; he left the scene of violence and continued the mission God had given him. Protecting life is not weakness; it is wisdom.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives peace, help us respect each other even in conflict, and keep our quarrels from bursting out like water through a broken dam. Give us wisdom to set boundaries and grace to keep them. And if anyone is suffering under violence and control, protect their safety and lead them to help. Amen.
teach: However intense a game gets, it still has rules; without rules it isn't a game, it's a brawl. Conflict between husband and wife is normal, but it needs boundaries. Proverbs says: “The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14). When a dam springs a small leak and isn't dealt with early, it soon bursts. We need agreements in place before our emotions run out of control.

Together, you can set some “fair fighting rules”: talk about one issue at a time; don't dredge up the past; no personal attacks, name-calling, or comparisons; never threaten divorce; when you need a break, say so, and agree on a time to come back and talk; as much as possible, don't argue heatedly in front of children or others. Proverbs says: “It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife” (Proverbs 20:3). This isn't avoiding problems; it's keeping problems from turning into war.

Peace takes effort from both people, and some situations are no longer “conflict” at all. If one spouse uses physical violence, intimidation, sexual coercion, financial control, or ongoing humiliation and isolation, that is abuse and control. It is not submission, and it is not something you are meant to endure; forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. Please put safety first and contact a pastor you trust, a professional counselor, or a local support service as soon as possible.
q: When we argue, which boundary do I cross most often?
Do I treat my spouse as an opponent to defeat, rather than a partner in solving the problem?
talk: Together, write down three “fair fighting rules” for our home, and both sign your names.
When we need a break, how would you like me to say so? How soon do we agree to come back and talk?
acts: Write down three “fair fighting rules” with your spouse
If you disagree today, stick to “one issue at a time”
If you are experiencing violence or control, reach out to someone you trust for help today
lessons.noon: “It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife” — Lord, right now make me a peacemaker.

lessons.title: Smoothing the Rough Edges: Growing Through Conflict
lessons.theme: God can make conflict a tool that shapes us to be more like Christ

v: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations,
knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

lessons.still: Look back on this week: the source of conflict, from “want” to “must-have,” asking God to search us, rules for arguing. Quietly thank the Lord that he is still at work in your conflicts. Say to him: “Lord, make even our friction a tool in your hands to shape us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, conflict is trouble; from God's point of view, conflict is a chisel. Change your mindset and your life will change: when we stop asking “How do I win?” and start asking “What does God want me to learn?”, conflict turns from a battlefield where both lose into a training ground where both grow—and we become overcomers together.
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times, and at that very moment, “The Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61). Peter remembered the Lord's words, went out, and wept bitterly. It was Peter's most painful moment, and also the beginning of the real turning point in his life. Jesus let failure expose Peter's weakness, and then, with a look of love, led him toward repentance and renewal.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that you are still at work in our conflicts. Make every point of friction an opportunity for our faith to be tested and to produce endurance, so that we become more and more like your Son. Help us no longer be afraid of conflict, nor hurt each other in it, but let you smooth our rough edges, so that we become an overcoming couple together. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: The smooth pebbles in a riverbed were once jagged chunks of rock. Only after years of flowing water and bumping against one another did they become round and smooth. Conflict in marriage can be like that. When two people with different backgrounds and personalities live together, they will bump into each other; but bumping isn't necessarily bad. What matters is how we face it, and whom we let take charge of the process.

James says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance” (James 1:2–3). The friction in marriage is one such testing. God's aim is not just that we have a little less conflict, but that we “may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James 1:4)—more and more like Jesus. In every conflict God is asking: Will you let me change you through this?

Conflict exposes the selfish desires, pride, and fear in our hearts—things we normally can't see rise to the surface under friction. It hurts, but it is also an opportunity: once we see, we can repent; once we repent, we can be renewed. Next week we will learn how to take the initiative to reconcile. Today, let's look at conflict with new eyes: it isn't necessarily a sign that our marriage has failed; it can actually be the beginning of growth.
q: Thinking of a past conflict, what did God later change in me through it?
In a current point of friction, what lesson might God want me to learn?
talk: Was there a conflict that actually helped us understand each other better afterward? What did we do right that time?
Which idea from this week's lessons most changed how you see conflict?
acts: Write down a way God helped you grow after a conflict, and share it with your spouse
When friction comes today, ask: “What does God want me to learn?”
Say to your spouse: “Thank you for growing together with me.”
lessons.noon: “the testing of your faith produces endurance” — Lord, right now use our friction to make us more like you.

mem.t: leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

s: Take a walk or share a drink together and talk about the homes you each grew up in: after the adults argued, how did they usually make up (or did they never make up at all)?
Together, write the five steps to reconcile—Stop · See · Own · Ask · Act—on a card and put it somewhere visible at home.
Agree on your family's own “pause signal” and a “reconciliation gesture,” such as holding hands, a hug, or making a cup of tea together.
Hold hands and pray: “Lord, make our home a place where we are quick to reconcile.”

lessons.title: Leave Your Gift and First Be Reconciled
lessons.theme: In God's eyes, reconciliation matters more than the gift—and it comes first

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

lessons.still: Be still and consider whether there is something between you and your spouse right now that hasn't been dealt with—perhaps just a cold remark or an unanswered message. You don't need to rush to fix it. Just say to the Lord: “Lord, I place this before you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind “waiting for the other person to come first” there is often a hidden thought: I want to win—or at least not lose. That is the self-ruled life. Pride provokes pride; when both are waiting, the relationship freezes. Humility draws out humility; when one person gets up first, the other heart begins to melt too. Going first to reconcile is not admitting defeat; it is letting Jesus reign.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said that a man with a hundred sheep who loses one will leave the ninety-nine and “go after the one that was lost, until he found it” (Luke 15:4). The shepherd doesn't stand still waiting for the sheep to come back on its own; he gets up and goes looking. Jesus is that kind of shepherd: he doesn't wait for us to turn back first—he comes looking first. Reconciliation doesn't have to wait for the perfect mood; love gets up first.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that while we were still far from you, you came looking for us first. We confess that we often hold our gift in our hands while setting reconciliation aside; we often wait for the other person to speak first, unwilling to get up first ourselves. Give us the courage to be reconciled first, and let the worship in our home begin with our reconciliation with each other. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Jesus paints a surprising picture: someone is already standing at the altar, holding a gift for God, when he suddenly remembers that his brother has something against him. Jesus' instruction is: “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). For the Galileans listening, the temple was far away in Jerusalem, yet Jesus said: put down the gift and go back first. In God's eyes, reconciliation matters more than ritual.

Notice that the text says “your brother has anything against you” (Matthew 5:23), not “you have something against your brother.” In other words, even if I feel the fault isn't entirely mine, once I know the other person is hurt, I am the one to get up and go. The most common deadlock in marriage is “waiting”: waiting for the other to apologize first, waiting for the other to soften first. When both are waiting, the home is like two cars nose to nose in a narrow lane—neither will back up, so neither can get out.

So this week we'll learn five simple steps to reconcile: Stop (pause and pray first), See (see your own part), Own (admit your own wrong first), Ask (ask for forgiveness, and forgive), Act (take one step of reconciliation). It isn't a formula, but a set of signposts that point the way when our emotions are churning. Every step starts with “me,” because change begins with me; and the strength for every step comes from the Lord who first came to reconcile with us.
q: Right now, is there something I know my spouse is hurt about, yet I keep waiting for them to speak first?
How much do I usually need to “win” before I'm willing to reconcile first?
talk: Think back to the last time we made up. Who took the first step? How did that step feel to you?
After an argument, how would you most like me to come close to you first? (If your spouse can't join you for now, write down the first sentence you'd like to say to them.)
acts: Think of one small thing that hasn't been reconciled, and bring it up first today
Write “Stop · See · Own · Ask · Act” in your phone's notes
Say to your spouse: “If I've upset you, I want to know.”
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” — Lord, right now I am willing to get up first and walk toward reconciliation.

lessons.title: Stop: Pause and Pray First
lessons.theme: Stop before the quarrel breaks out, and hand your words to God first

v: The heart of the righteous weighs answers, but the mouth of the wicked gushes out evil.
Then the king said to me, “What is your request?” So I prayed to the God of heaven.

lessons.still: Breathe in slowly, then breathe out slowly. Repeat three times. Imagine taking your foot off the gas and gently pressing the brake. Say to the Lord: “Lord, before I open my mouth, please speak to me first.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our quickest reactions in an argument usually come from the self-ruled life: I want to strike back now, clarify now, prove I'm right now. Stopping to pray means giving up the throne in that very instant and admitting, “Lord, you are King, not my emotions.” A single silent prayer is the smallest yet most powerful step toward the self-emptied life.
lessons.jesus: Before the momentous decision of choosing the twelve apostles, Jesus “went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). He didn't act on a passing feeling; he stopped first and went to the Father. If even the Son of God did this, how much more do we need to stop and pray before saying harsh words when our emotions are churning.
lessons.pray: God of heaven, you hear our shortest silent prayers. In the moment we want to strike back, remind us to stop first and turn our hearts to you. Set a guard over our mouths, so that the waters of strife are not let loose in our home. We want you to reign, not our emotions. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Proverbs says: “The heart of the righteous weighs answers” (Proverbs 15:28). To weigh is to consider and measure in the heart before letting the words out. The most hurtful words in an argument are usually the ones that burst straight out of our emotions without being weighed—like a small crack in a levee: the water pushes harder and harder until nothing can hold it back. The best moment is not after the flood but the instant before the words leave our mouth: Stop.

Stopping is not the silent treatment, nor is it running away. It is first handing the steering wheel to God. Nehemiah was standing before the king of Persia when the king suddenly asked, “What is your request?” Scripture continues: “So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 2:4). The prayer was so short the king didn't even notice, yet it shaped every sentence Nehemiah said next. We can do the same in an argument: first say in our hearts, “Lord, help me,” and then speak.

In practice, “Stop” can be three small actions: close your mouth for five seconds, take a deep breath, and silently pray one sentence. If emotions are running too high, you can also say gently, “I need to stop for a moment. Let's talk again in a little while.” The key is: we stop in order to come back, not in order to leave. Stopping moves us from automatic reactions back to depending on the Holy Spirit. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself.
q: In conflict, at what moment do I most often “breach the levee”? Is it a word, a facial expression, or a tone of voice?
The next time my emotions rise, what short sentence do I want to pray silently to God?
talk: Can we agree on a “pause signal”? For example, a gesture or a phrase that means, “Let's stop for a moment and each pray.”
When I need to stop for a moment, how can I say it so that you don't feel rejected or abandoned?
acts: Write down a sentence you will pray silently during conflict
Agree with your spouse on a pause gesture or signal
Before speaking today, pause for five seconds and notice your heart's reaction
lessons.noon: “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” — Lord, before I open my mouth, please take charge of my heart.

lessons.title: See: See Your Own Part
lessons.theme: Remove the beam from your own eye first, and then you can see clearly

v: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?
Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.
Who can discern his errors? Forgive me from hidden errors.

lessons.still: Imagine a mirror placed in front of you. For this moment, don't think about what your spouse did wrong. Just gently ask the Lord: “Lord, in our recent conflict, what was my part? Please gently help me see it.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on others. Self-ruled eyes only look outward: “It's all their problem.” Self-emptied eyes look inward first: “Lord, what is my part?” When husband and wife both look at themselves first, blame turns into responsibility, and the two go from opponents back to companions.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper, Jesus said that one of the disciples would betray him. The disciples didn't point at each other; instead “each began to ask him, ‘It isn't me, is it, Lord?’” (Matthew 26:22). Jesus' words led each one to examine himself first. In conflict, we too can ask the Lord first: “Is it me? What is my part?”
lessons.pray: God who searches the heart, we often see each other's specks yet can't see our own beams. Shine your gentle light on us, so that we see our own part first and stop rushing to point out each other's faults. Heal our eyes, so that we see clearly and love more deeply. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Jesus used a picture so exaggerated it's almost funny: a person with a beam stuck in his eye, holding tweezers to pick a speck out of his brother's eye. “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but don't consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). In marriage we see our spouse's speck in perfect detail because we live up close every day, but we can't see our own beam—because it's right in front of our eyes.

Jesus didn't say the brother has no speck, or that the speck doesn't need to be dealt with. He was talking about order: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly” (Matthew 7:5). In conflict, the step “See” means asking first: In this situation, what is my part? Maybe it was my tone, my lateness, my distraction, or maybe I brought my work stress home. Even if it's only ten percent, that ten percent is mine to take responsibility for.

Seeing ourselves isn't easy, because the human heart is an expert at defending itself. The psalmist honestly admits he has blind spots, so he prays: “Who can discern his errors? Forgive me from hidden errors” (Psalm 19:12). We aren't putting ourselves under a magnifying glass to condemn ourselves; we're inviting the God who loves us to shine his light on us. His light is like the lamp in a doctor's hand—not to shame, but to heal. Only those who know they are seen by God find the courage to see themselves.
q: In our most recent conflict, if I could only talk about “my part,” what would I say?
Which of my spouse's “specks” do I notice most easily? Could it be reflecting a beam of my own?
talk: Each of you say one sentence: “In our last argument, my part was…” Talk only about yourself, not your spouse.
When you hear me own my part, how do you feel inside?
acts: Write down “my part” in your most recent conflict
Today, resist the urge to correct your spouse at least once
Use Psalm 19:12 as your bedtime prayer
lessons.noon: “First remove the beam out of your own eye” — Lord, help me see myself first, and then see others.

lessons.title: Own and Ask: Admit the Wrong and Ask for Forgiveness
lessons.theme: Confess specifically, ask sincerely for forgiveness, and be ready to forgive

v: When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.
For day and night your hand was heavy on me. My strength was sapped in the heat of summer. Selah.
I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

lessons.still: Pause and think of something you know in your heart you did wrong but haven't yet admitted. Don't be afraid—God already knows. Tell him: “Lord, I don't want to hide this anymore. Give me the courage to admit my wrong.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Admitting we're wrong is hard because the self is afraid of losing face and losing status. But the gospel tells us our worth is not in never making mistakes, but in being loved and forgiven by Christ. People who stand in grace no longer need to protect themselves, and can say freely: “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?”
lessons.jesus: One of the criminals crucified with Jesus admitted that he was being punished justly, and then pleaded, “Lord, remember me when you come into your Kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Jesus immediately promised him that today he would be with him in paradise. Admitting our wrong and calling on the Lord brings not humiliation but the welcome of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord who forgives sin, thank you that when we confess our transgressions, you forgive the iniquity of our sin. Take away the pride and excuses in our hearts, so that we can confess specifically and ask for forgiveness sincerely. Soften our hearts too, so that when the other admits a wrong, we forgive as you have forgiven us. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: For a time David sinned and refused to admit it. He describes what that was like: “When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). People who won't admit their wrongs look tough on the outside but are exhausted inside. It's the same between husband and wife: an unspoken wrong is like a small pebble in your shoe—not fatal, but every step aches a little. Only when David said, “I will confess my transgressions to the LORD” (Psalm 32:5) was the burden finally lifted.

There are good and bad ways to “own” a wrong. A bad apology comes with a “but”: “I'm sorry, but you also…” That's really just blaming in a different way. A good apology is specific and makes no excuses: “I was wrong to interrupt you and put you down in front of our friends just now.” Naming the specific thing shows that I have really seen it; leaving out the “but” shows that I am willing to take full responsibility for my part.

After owning comes “asking”: “Will you forgive me?” This sentence hands the initiative to the other person and reminds both of us that reconciliation takes two hearts. The Lord's Prayer says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). So “asking” has two sides: I ask my spouse for forgiveness, and I am ready to forgive them. Those who are forgiven learn to forgive, and those who forgive understand all the more what grace it is that they themselves have been forgiven.
q: Is there something I have “kept silent” about in my heart that still aches?
What kind of “but” most often slips into my apologies?
talk: For you, what kind of apology feels the most sincere?
Let's practice once: each of you name one small thing, say “I was wrong. Will you forgive me?” and then respond, “I forgive you.”
acts: Apologize specifically for one small thing, without adding “but”
Practice saying: “Will you forgive me?”
Respond to your spouse's apology: “Thank you. I forgive you.”
lessons.noon: “I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn't hide my iniquity.” — Lord, right now I stop hiding and open my heart before you.

lessons.title: Act: Take One Step of Reconciliation
lessons.theme: Reconciliation in the heart needs to show up in a visible action

v: He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.

lessons.still: Think: if you were to do one small act of reconciliation for your spouse today, what would it be? A hot cup of tea, a hug, a little note? Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, let my reconciliation be not only in my heart, but also in my hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A changed life changes how we live, and a changed way of living changes our relationships. Reconciliation in the heart without action is like a letter written but never mailed. The self-emptied person doesn't just say “Forget it”; they are willing to walk over first and reach out first. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than saving face.
lessons.jesus: Thomas refused to believe the Lord had risen. Eight days later, Jesus came again specifically for him and said, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands” (John 20:27). Jesus didn't just accept Thomas in his heart; he came close and restored him with a concrete action. This is exactly what “Act” looks like: letting love be seen and touched.
lessons.pray: God who reconciles, thank you for leading us this week to learn Stop, See, Own, Ask, and Act. Let us be reconciled not only in our hearts, but willing to come close to each other through action. When we pull back, grow proud, or want to wait for the other to come first, remind us that you came to us first, long ago. May our home be full of the embraces of reconciliation. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Jacob had once tricked his brother Esau out of his blessing and lived as a fugitive for twenty years. On the way home, he finally had to face that broken relationship. Scripture says he “bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother” (Genesis 33:3). Jacob didn't just think about reconciling; he walked toward his brother with his own body and expressed humility through action. Step by step, bow after bow—this is what reconciliation looks like: not a fine speech, but a road walked toward the other person.

Then something unexpected happened: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him” (Genesis 33:4), and the two of them wept. Jacob said, “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10). In the embrace of reconciliation, there is the light of God's face. Between husband and wife, “Act” is often one simple action: a hug, a meal your spouse loves, a note that says “Thank you for forgiving me”—so that the reconciliation in our hearts can be seen and touched.

Let's put this week together: Stop (pause and pray first), See (see your own part), Own (admit your own wrong first), Ask (ask for forgiveness, and forgive), Act (take one step of reconciliation). The Reconcile toolkit in the app will walk with us step by step. A reminder, too: these five steps are meant for two people who respect each other. If pushing, hitting, threats, or intimidation appear in a conflict, first make sure you are safe and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. That is not something you can carry alone with five steps.
q: Of the five steps, which one is hardest for me? Why?
Between my spouse and me, is there a place where we've “made up in our hearts” but haven't yet taken action?
talk: For you, what kind of reconciling action most makes you feel, “We've really made up”?
The next time we have a conflict, which of the five steps do we want to start practicing together? (If your spouse can't join you for now, write down the step you want to practice first yourself.)
acts: Do one specific small act of reconciliation for your spouse
Open the Reconcile toolkit and walk through the five steps
Hug your spouse and say: “We're on the same team.”
lessons.noon: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him” — Lord, right now make me the one who reaches out first.

mem.t: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,

s: Pick an evening to take a walk together. As you watch the sun go down, talk about what the people in your childhood homes were like when they got angry.
Take turns finishing this sentence: “When I'm angry, what I really need most inside is…”
Together, write down your family's “cool-down agreement”: either of you can call a pause, how long the pause lasts, and how you'll come back to talk again.
At sunset, hold hands and pray: “Lord, we won't carry today's anger into the night. We place it all in your hands.”

lessons.title: Anger Itself Is Not a Sin
lessons.theme: Anger is like a warning light; what matters is how we respond to it

v: “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,

lessons.still: Be still and recall the last time you were angry. No need to rush to blame yourself or defend yourself. Just tell the Lord honestly: “Lord, I was really angry then. Please help me understand my own heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the warning light of anger comes on, the self-ruled person's first thought is, “You made me angry.” The self-emptied person first asks, “Lord, what is this anger telling me?” When our focus turns from others back to ourselves, and then from ourselves to Jesus, anger turns from a destructive force into an opportunity to grow.
lessons.jesus: In the synagogue on the Sabbath, people coldly watched to see whether Jesus would heal. Scripture says that “he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts” (Mark 3:5). His anger held grief and love, and then he healed the man. Jesus' anger was not for himself, but so that a person could be made whole.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are a God slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness. We confess that our anger is often mixed with our own pride and needs. Teach us to stop when the warning light of anger comes on and listen for your voice. Help us not to let anger stay overnight, and not to let it turn into bitterness in our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: When a warning light comes on in a car's dashboard, a wise driver doesn't smash the light or pretend not to see it; they pull over and check the engine. Anger is like that light. It tells us something is wrong—maybe we've been offended or ignored, or we've seen injustice. Paul says, “Be angry, and don't sin” (Ephesians 4:26). He doesn't say, “Never be angry,” but rather, when you are angry, don't cross the line.

Paul is quoting the Greek translation of Psalm 4. Scripture often says God is “slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6), yet he also becomes angry at sin and injustice. So anger itself is not sin; the question is where it comes from and where it goes. Our anger is often mixed with the self-ruled life: not about God's justice, but because “my” plans were disrupted, “my” pride was wounded, “my” needs weren't met.

Paul immediately adds: “Don't let the sun go down on your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26). In ancient Israel, sunset marked the end of the day. The point is: don't let today's anger cross over into tomorrow; don't let it stay overnight in your heart and ferment. Anger is like a glass of milk left on the table—leave it overnight and it turns sour. Facing it early and handing it to God early is the best protection for a marriage.
q: The last time I was angry, what was that “warning light” trying to tell me?
Is my anger more often about God's justice, or about “my” plans, pride, or needs?
talk: In the home you grew up in, what were the adults usually like when they got angry? How has that shaped who you are today?
When I get angry, what's the first thing you feel? Please tell me gently—I'm willing to listen.
acts: Note one moment today when you felt angry, and why
When angry, first say in your heart: “Lord, what is this light telling me?”
Before bed, check in with your spouse: “Are we okay today?”
lessons.noon: “Be angry, and don't sin. Don't let the sun go down on your wrath” — Lord, right now I hand you the anger in my heart.

lessons.title: Why Are You Angry?
lessons.theme: Beneath anger often lie hurt, fear, and unmet expectations

v: but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell.
The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”

lessons.still: Imagine God, like a loving father, sitting down beside you and asking softly, “Why are you angry?” Don't rush to answer. Let the question rest in your heart for a while, then slowly tell him your answer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The root of anger is often the self-ruled life: “I” wasn't valued; “my” expectations fell through. When God asked Cain “why,” he was calling him to return to his rightful place and see his own heart. When we answer God's question honestly, we no longer just vent our emotions on our spouse; we can name the real needs deep in our hearts.
lessons.jesus: Mary was weeping at the empty tomb. The risen Jesus did not reveal who he was right away, but first asked her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” (John 20:15). He cared not only about the tears on the surface but about the heart beneath them. Jesus is willing to ask us just as gently, helping us see the real needs beneath our emotions.
lessons.pray: Loving Father, thank you that you see not only our anger but also the hurting heart beneath it. Help us answer your question honestly, and help us see the needs below the surface in our spouse. When sin crouches at the door, give us the strength to rule over it, so that anger does not hurt the people we love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: When Cain's offering was not accepted, “Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell” (Genesis 4:5). God did not rebuke him immediately; instead he asked, “Why are you angry?” (Genesis 4:6). It is a question full of grace. God invited Cain to look inside: Beneath the anger, was it jealousy? Shame? A feeling of not being valued? God's question is meant to lead us from the surface of our emotions into the depths of the heart.

Anger is like the tip of an iceberg; beneath the surface there is often something bigger: hurt, fear, disappointment, exhaustion. A wife flares up because her husband came home late again, but underneath may be, “I feel like I don't matter.” A husband explodes at a single criticism, but underneath may be, “I'm afraid I'm not good enough.” When we only see the anger above the water, we keep fighting; when we see the needs below the water, we can truly draw close to each other.

God went on to warn Cain: “sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it” (Genesis 4:7). Sin is like a wild animal crouching at the door, waiting for anger to open it. Cain didn't listen, and his anger moved from his face to his hands, and the end was tragedy. Today we have a choice: let anger open the door to sin, or bring our anger to God and let him master it.
q: If God asked me today, “Why are you angry?”, what would be my most honest answer?
Beneath my anger, which feeling is most often hiding: hurt, fear, disappointment, or exhaustion?
talk: Each of you finish this sentence: “When I'm angry with you, what's below the surface is often…”
Next time I'm angry, how can you gently ask me, “What's below the surface?” without making me feel analyzed?
acts: Write down the real feeling beneath your most recent anger
Tell your spouse one need from deep in your heart, instead of a complaint
When angry, ask yourself: “Why am I angry?”
lessons.noon: “Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” — Lord, right now help me rule over the anger in my heart.

lessons.title: Slow to Anger
lessons.theme: Being slow to anger is not weakness but a greater strength

v: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.
Don’t be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.

lessons.still: Picture a strong city with its gates shut tight. Then picture your own heart as a city that needs guarding. Say to the Lord: “Lord, more than winning an argument, I want to guard my own heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: A quick temper is the self rushing to protect itself and be in charge; ruling our own spirit means yielding the throne of the heart to Jesus. Pride provokes pride: when one person flares up, the other heats up too. Humility draws out humility: when one person slows down, the temperature of the whole home comes down as well.
lessons.jesus: People insulted Jesus to his face, saying he had a demon. Jesus didn't explode or strike back; he simply answered calmly, “I don't have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me” (John 8:49). He spoke the truth without losing control. Jesus shows us that ruling our own spirit is more powerful than winning an argument.
lessons.pray: God who is slow to anger, thank you for bearing with our weakness again and again. Lengthen the distance between our feelings and our reactions, and give the Holy Spirit room to work in our hearts. We don't want to win arguments but lose each other. Help us rule our own spirits, and reign in our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Ecclesiastes says, “Don't be hasty in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools” (Ecclesiastes 7:9). Hasty anger is like a firecracker with a short fuse: it goes off at the slightest spark, and those nearby are the most likely to get hurt. At home, the person who is loudest and best at winning arguments is often not the strongest. You may win the argument but lose a heart. The truly strong person is the one who can control their temper.

Proverbs also says, “He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly” (Proverbs 14:29). In Hebrew, “slow to anger” literally means “long of nose”: people in ancient times pictured anger as hot breath snorting from the nostrils, so anger that comes slowly was called a “long nose.” This doesn't mean having no feelings, but that there is some distance between feeling and reacting. We can ask God to lengthen that distance, giving the Holy Spirit room to work.

How can we lengthen the distance? One way is to count God's grace in your heart: How patient God has been with me! I fail again and again, yet he has not been angry with me. Another way is to say it out loud: “I'm feeling a bit angry right now. I need a little time to think before I speak.” Naming anger protects both of you better than unleashing it. Slowing down is not weakness; it is self-control in love.
q: In our home, am I more often “the one who wins the argument” or “the one who rules their own spirit”?
How long is my “distance” between feeling and reacting? In which situations is it especially short?
talk: When do you feel I'm especially quick to get impatient? How can we slow down together at those times?
When you say, “I'm feeling a bit angry right now,” how would you like me to respond?
acts: Practice saying today: “I'm feeling a bit angry right now. I want to think first.”
Remember one time God was patient with you, and write it down
Before responding to your spouse, slowly count to ten
lessons.noon: “He who is slow to anger has great understanding” — Lord, right now help me guard my own heart.

lessons.title: The Wisdom of a Cool-Down Time
lessons.theme: We pause in order to come back; we cool down in order to love better

v: A fool vents all of his anger, but a wise man brings himself under control.
Stand in awe, and don’t sin. Search your own heart on your bed, and be still. Selah.

lessons.still: Picture a kettle that has just boiled, its lid rattling. Pour it into a cup right now and someone could easily get burned. Let it settle in your heart for a moment. Say to the Lord: “Lord, when I'm boiling inside, teach me to wait.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The purpose of a cool-down time is not the silent treatment or punishing the other person, but moving from “living from the head by ourselves” back to “living from the heart by the Spirit.” Live from the heart and find joy; live from the head and find worry. When we give ourselves to God during the pause, we come back not as two colliding emotions, but as two people quieted by God, facing the problem together.
lessons.jesus: After feeding the five thousand, the crowds still pressed around Jesus, but he first sent them away and “went up into the mountain by himself to pray” (Matthew 14:23). Amid crowds and pressure, Jesus knew how to keep a quiet time alone with the Father. Pausing is not running away; it is returning to the Father to be strengthened again.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives peace, when our hearts are boiling, teach us to wait and not vent all our anger. Make our pauses times of prayer, not the start of a cold war. Wherever there is anything unsafe in our home, protect us and lead us to seek help. May your peace rule in our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Proverbs says, “A fool vents all of his anger, but a wise man brings himself under control” (Proverbs 29:11). Bringing ourselves under control doesn't mean swallowing our anger and pretending everything is fine; it means reining it in first, so it doesn't explode at the most hurtful moment. Like water just off the boil: don't rush to pour it; wait for the temperature to drop a little, and you can brew a good cup of tea. In marriage, wise couples understand this: some things are best said after we've calmed down.

The psalm says, “Search your own heart on your bed, and be still” (Psalm 4:4). A cool-down time is giving yourself a stretch of stillness. In practice it can look like this: one person says, “I need to pause for a bit,” and both agree on a time to come back and talk. During the pause, don't rehearse comebacks in your head; instead pray, take a walk, breathe deeply, and ask God, “What is my part?” When the agreed time comes, be sure to come back.

“Don't let the sun go down on your wrath” doesn't mean every argument must be fully talked through before bed. Sometimes both of you are exhausted, and forcing the conversation only makes things worse. But you can say before bed, “We're not finished talking, but I love you. Let's talk again tomorrow.” And let's be clear: if anger turns into throwing things, pushing, hitting, threats, or intimidation, that is no longer anger; it is violence. In that case, please first get to a safe place, and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. Safety always comes first.
q: When I need to pause, do I usually give the silent treatment, walk away, or truly become quiet and pray?
During a pause, is my heart more often rehearsing comebacks or seeking God?
talk: Let's make a “cool-down agreement”: Who can call a pause? How long does it last? How will we come back?
If we haven't finished talking by bedtime, what sentence can we use to reassure each other that love hasn't gone anywhere?
acts: Write down your cool-down agreement with your spouse
When you pause today, take a walk or pray for five minutes
Before bed, say: “We're not finished talking, but I love you.”
lessons.noon: “a wise man brings himself under control” — Lord, right now quiet my heart as I wait for you.

lessons.title: Give No Place to the Devil
lessons.theme: Anger left unresolved becomes a foothold for the enemy

v: and don’t give place to the devil.
looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,
A wrathful man stirs up contention, but one who is slow to anger appeases strife.

lessons.still: Imagine the door of your home left open a crack, with a cold draft blowing through. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, is there a door in my heart that hasn't been properly shut because of anger?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Giving place to the devil means letting the self keep its grip on anger: “I have a right to be angry. I don't want to forgive.” Letting Jesus reign means surrendering that right. When we stop clinging to anger, the enemy loses his foothold, and the Holy Spirit has room to produce the fruit of peace and gentleness.
lessons.jesus: When Peter urged Jesus not to take the road to the cross, Jesus turned at once and said, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 16:23). Even though the words came from a close disciple, Jesus saw the foothold the enemy was looking for and shut the door on the spot. Jesus is our example: give the enemy no place to set foot in our hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord, we don't want to give any place to the devil. Search our hearts for all bitterness, wrath, and unresolved anger, and wash it clean with your precious blood. Make us people who calm strife, and let the Holy Spirit move freely in our home. We bring every bout of anger to your cross. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
