teach: Right after Paul says, “Don't let the sun go down on your wrath,” he adds, “and don't give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:27). “Place” here means a spot, a position—like giving the enemy a place to set his foot. One unresolved bout of anger is like leaving the front door open a crack. The gap isn't big, but it's enough for the enemy to wedge his foot in—to stir up trouble, accuse, and drive a wedge between us. The devil doesn't need to tear down the whole house; a single foothold is enough.

Paul then lists a series of things: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). The list is like a downward slope: bitterness takes root in the heart, grows into wrath, erupts as anger, rises into outcry, and ends in slander and malice. The starting point is often just one unresolved bout of anger, as Hebrews warns: “lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you” (Hebrews 12:15). So the best time to stop is at the top of the slope.

This week we've learned: anger is a warning light; ask, “Why am I angry?”; one who rules his spirit is better than one who takes a city; use a cool-down time to wait on God; don't let anger stay overnight. Proverbs says, “A wrathful man stirs up contention, but one who is slow to anger appeases strife” (Proverbs 15:18). May we all become people who calm strife, bringing every bout of anger to the cross, giving no place at all to the devil and the whole house to the Holy Spirit.
q: Is there some “unresolved anger” in my heart that is slowly turning into bitterness?
On the slope of bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander, where do I most often stop?
talk: Of this week's five lessons, which idea has helped you most? Why?
Is there a door in our home that hasn't been properly shut because of anger, one we need to pray together to close? (If your spouse can't join you for now, write down your prayer for that door.)
acts: Write down one anger still in your heart, and give it to God in prayer
Say one thing to your spouse today that calms strife
Read Ephesians 4:31–32 together and bless each other
lessons.noon: “don't give place to the devil” — Lord, right now I shut the door on anger and give my heart to you.

mem.t: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

date.t: A Walk to Lay Down Burdens
s: Go for a walk outdoors together. Each of you pick up a small stone and carry it with you, as a symbol of a small burden you are still carrying in your heart.
Sit down and take turns sharing: this past year, what is one thing you are most grateful your spouse forgave you for?
Each of you silently hand over to God whatever your stone represents (you don't need to say what it is), then gently set the stone down or drop it into the water.
Hold hands and read Colossians 3:13 together, then pray: “Lord, just as you have forgiven us, help us forgive each other in the same way.”

lessons.title: Those Who Are Forgiven Can Forgive
lessons.theme: The power to forgive comes from having first been forgiven by God far, far more

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’

lessons.still: Be still and think about the things God has forgiven you. You don't have to list them one by one; just let the gratitude of being forgiven slowly rise in your heart. Softly say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you for forgiving me so much.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: People who refuse to forgive are really sitting on the judgment seat, judging others by their own standards—leaving our rightful place and taking God's. Remembering that I, too, am a forgiven sinner is how I return to my rightful place. Let people be people, and let God be God, and forgiveness will flow naturally out of grace.
lessons.jesus: When a paralyzed man was lowered through the roof to Jesus, Jesus' first words were not “Get up and walk,” but “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2:5). Jesus knew that a person's deepest need is to be forgiven. We are able to forgive others because we first heard these words from him.
lessons.pray: Merciful Father, thank you for canceling our debt of ten thousand talents. We truly don't deserve it. Help us always remember the grace of being forgiven, so that we stop grabbing each other by the throat to collect what we're owed. Put your mercy in our hearts, so that we can forgive each other from the heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Peter asked Jesus, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). He probably thought he was being quite generous. But Jesus said, “I don't tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). Jesus isn't asking us to carry a tally counter and stop at four hundred ninety. He is saying that forgiveness isn't a coupon that eventually runs out; it is a way of life.

Then Jesus told a parable. A servant owed his master “ten thousand talents”—an astronomical sum that a laborer could never repay in a lifetime—yet the master canceled it all. As soon as this servant went out, he met a fellow servant who owed him “one hundred denarii,” and he grabbed him by the throat and demanded payment. The master confronted him: “Shouldn't you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33). The gap between those two debts is the gap between how God forgives us and how we forgive others.

This parable teaches us that forgiveness doesn't start with “Does he deserve it?” but with “How much have I been forgiven?” When we remember that we owed God ten thousand talents, the hundred denarii our spouse owes us no longer looks so enormous. That doesn't mean our spouse's wrongs are unimportant or painless. It means we hold a far greater grace in our hands, enough to cover this smaller debt. Only those who know they are forgiven have the power to forgive.
q: Do I remember that I owed God “ten thousand talents”? Or do I often feel I didn't owe him much?
Am I still holding on to some “hundred denarii” my spouse owes me?
talk: Share a time when your spouse forgave you and it deeply moved you.
For you, what is the hardest part of forgiving? The pain, the unfairness, or the fear that it will happen again?
acts: Write down three things God has forgiven you, and give thanks for them
Think of one “hundred denarii” your spouse owes you, and hand it to God
Say to your spouse: “Thank you for forgiving me in the past.”
lessons.noon: “I don't tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” — Lord, right now I remember how much you have forgiven me.

lessons.title: What Forgiveness Is Not
lessons.theme: Forgiveness is not forgetting, not excusing, and not staying in danger

v: Be careful. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him.
If he sins against you seven times in the day, and seven times returns, saying, ‘I repent,’ you shall forgive him.”

lessons.still: Breathe deeply and quietly. If there is a deep wound in your heart, know that God sees it and cares about it. Say to the Lord: “Lord, help me understand how you want me to forgive.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Forgiveness is laying down the self's right to take revenge and make the other person pay, and handing judgment back to God. But forgiveness does not mean laying down the truth, or laying down the safety and dignity God has given us. Letting God be God means trusting his justice and also accepting the protections he has put in place: the church, pastors, professional help, and the law.
lessons.jesus: Jesus healed a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years. Later he found him in the temple and said to him, “Behold, you are made well. Sin no more” (John 5:14). His grace is free, and his warning is real. Jesus shows us that grace does not excuse sin, and truth does not lose its mercy.
lessons.pray: Righteous and merciful Lord, thank you for helping us understand what forgiveness truly is. Help us forgive without excusing sin, and lay down revenge without laying down the truth. Protect everyone who is being harmed in their home; lead them to a safe place and to people who are willing to help them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Many people are afraid to forgive because they misunderstand what forgiveness is. First, forgiveness is not forgetting. Human memory is not a computer where you press delete and it's gone. Forgiveness means remembering, yet choosing not to use it to attack the other person anymore. Second, forgiveness is not excusing. Jesus said, “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). Forgiveness and naming a wrong can exist side by side; forgiving does not mean saying, “It's fine, everything you did was right.”

Third, forgiveness does not mean instantly restoring trust. Forgiveness is me laying down my right to revenge, and that can be decided in a moment. Trust, however, has to be rebuilt by the other person over time and through actions—like a bridge washed away by a flood that has to be rebuilt one beam at a time. Fourth, forgiveness is not pretending we weren't hurt. We can weep and say at the same time, “Lord, I choose to forgive.” True forgiveness is precious precisely because the wound is real.

Most important of all: forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. If a marriage involves physical violence, verbal intimidation and humiliation, sexual coercion, financial control, or being cut off from family and friends, these are not things that forgiveness or submission can cover over. God does not want you to stay in danger. Please first make sure you and your family are safe; if necessary, leave for a safe place, and seek help from a pastor and from professionals. If you are in immediate danger, call the police right away. You can forgive from a safe distance, while letting the other person face the consequences they need to bear.
q: Which misunderstanding about forgiveness has kept me afraid of forgiving, or unwilling to forgive?
In my heart, have “forgiving” and “trusting again” become mixed up?
talk: How do you think forgiveness differs from “acting like it never happened”? Which one is more common in our home?
When I need to point out something you did wrong, how can I say it so that you feel I still love you and am willing to forgive you?
acts: Write down one misunderstanding you've had about forgiveness, and correct it with today's passage
Save the contact details of a pastor or counselor you trust
Pray for someone who has been hurt in their marriage
lessons.noon: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him.” — Lord, teach me to forgive in truth and in love.

lessons.title: Hand the Debt to the Righteous Lord
lessons.theme: Forgiveness means placing what my spouse owes me into God's hands

v: May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you.
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.

lessons.still: Imagine holding an IOU in your hand, with something your spouse owes you written on it. You're gripping it so tightly that your hand aches. Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, I want to hand this IOU to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Avenging ourselves is the self climbing onto the judgment throne; handing the debt to God is letting Jesus reign and letting God be God. When we stop being our spouse's judge, we can return to our rightful place as their companion. When our focus shifts from “what they owe me” to “what the Lord paid for me,” our hearts are set free.
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus suffered the deepest injustice, and at the end he cried with a loud voice, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). He did not avenge himself; he entrusted everything to the Father. Three days later, the Father raised him from the dead. Jesus shows us that whatever we entrust to God, God himself will take responsibility for.
lessons.pray: Righteous Lord, we hand you, one by one, the IOUs we have been holding in our hearts. We will no longer avenge ourselves, because you are more just than we are and you understand everything. When we want to take them back again, remind us that you have already paid a far greater debt for us. Help us overcome evil with good and live out your grace in our home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: In the original languages of the Bible, forgiveness is often linked with canceling a debt. When someone hurts us, it's as if we're holding an IOU in our hearts: “You owe me an apology,” “You owe me justice.” Not forgiving means holding on to that IOU, reminding the other person—and ourselves. The problem is, the longer we hold it, the more our hand aches; and the one bound by this IOU is often not the other person, but ourselves.

When Saul was hunting David down, David had a chance in a cave to take revenge with his own hands. Instead he said, “May the LORD judge between me and you, and may the LORD avenge me of you; but my hand will not be on you” (1 Samuel 24:12). Forgiveness doesn't say the debt doesn't exist; it hands the debt over to a more righteous Judge. Notice too: David forgave Saul, but he did not go back to Saul's side. He still kept a safe distance.

Peter describes how Jesus, when he suffered, “committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). In practice we can train ourselves like this: in prayer, name the debt specifically—“Lord, what he said that day hurt me”—and then say, “I hand this debt to you. I won't demand it from him anymore.” Some debts run deep; we hand them over and then take them back. Then hand them over again. Only a hand that has let go of the IOU is free to do something kind for our spouse.
q: Which “IOU” am I holding in my heart right now? How long have I been holding it?
Have I ever handed a debt to God and later taken it back?
talk: For you, what is the hardest part of “handing the debt to God”?
Is there one small thing we can pray about together today and hand over to God? (If your spouse can't join you for now, write it down on your own and give it to the Lord.)
acts: Write an “IOU,” pray over it, then tear it up
Do one small thing for your spouse today that overcomes evil with good
Memorize Colossians 3:13
lessons.noon: “committed himself to him who judges righteously” — Lord, right now I let go of the IOU and entrust it to you, the righteous One.

lessons.title: Forgiveness and Rebuilding Trust
lessons.theme: Forgiveness can be given at once; trust takes time to rebuild

v: Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.

lessons.still: Picture a bridge broken by a flood, and workers setting new posts one by one. Quietly say to the Lord: “Lord, some bridges between us haven't been repaired yet. Please be our builder.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Demanding, “I've already apologized, so you should trust me right away,” is one form of the self-ruled life; refusing to give the other person any chance to rebuild is another. The self-emptied person says, “I'm willing to bear the process of rebuilding,” and also, “I'm willing to give you room to rebuild.” Humility draws out humility, and the bridge can slowly be repaired.
lessons.jesus: Many people believed in Jesus when they saw his miracles, but Scripture says, “Jesus didn't entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone” (John 2:24). Jesus loves every person, yet he does not hand himself over into people's hands lightly. He shows us that love and wisdom do not conflict, and that forgiveness is not the same as blind trust.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for showing us in Joseph's story that forgiveness and wisdom can walk together. Help us forgive sincerely where forgiveness is needed, and rebuild patiently where rebuilding is needed. To the one who did wrong, give transparency and perseverance; to the one who was hurt, give healing and hope. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers and suffered injustice for more than a decade. Years later, when his brothers came to Egypt to buy grain, Joseph did not reveal himself right away. He tested them first to see whether they had truly changed. Only when he saw his brothers willing to take responsibility for their youngest brother Benjamin did he weep aloud and say, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt” (Genesis 45:4). Joseph's forgiveness was real, but rebuilding the relationship was a wise process.

Joseph told his brothers, “Now don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life” (Genesis 45:5). He didn't say, “You didn't sell me.” He named the harm clearly, but he also saw God's greater hand above the harm. That is mature forgiveness. Then Joseph wept as he embraced his brothers, and Scripture says, “After that his brothers talked with him” (Genesis 45:15). Through tears and time, the relationship was slowly restored.

In marriage, if one spouse has damaged trust—for example, through lying, hiding things, or betrayal—forgiveness can be today's choice, but trust has to be rebuilt by the one who did wrong through transparency, honesty, and consistent action. The hurt spouse can say, “I choose to forgive you. Let's walk the road of rebuilding together.” If the harm involves violence or ongoing control, rebuilding trust is not the first step—safety is. In that case, please seek help from a pastor and from professionals, and only talk about the future of the relationship once safety is secured.
q: In our relationship, is there a “bridge still under repair”? What role am I playing in the rebuilding?
Have I ever confused “forgiving” with “trusting right away,” and so put too much pressure on myself or my spouse?
talk: For you, what kinds of actions would best help you rebuild trust in me?
Which bridge between us has already been repaired? Let's thank God together for that restoration.
acts: Do one small thing that increases your spouse's trust in you
Do what you say: keep one small promise today
Pray together with your spouse for a bridge that is still under repair
lessons.noon: “God sent me before you to preserve life” — Lord, right now I trust that you can work something good above the harm.

lessons.title: Forgiving Yourself, Too
lessons.theme: Only by receiving God's forgiveness can we truly forgive others—and let ourselves go

v: I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins.
Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

lessons.still: Is there something you have already confessed to God, yet still won't let yourself off for? Quietly listen as the Lord says to you, “I have forgiven you.” Let those words stay in your heart a little longer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Refusing to let ourselves off may look like humility on the surface, but underneath, the self is often still in control: I want to pay it back myself, make up for it myself, decide for myself when it's enough. The gospel tells us that Jesus has already paid it all. The self-emptied life means handing even our guilt over to him, and letting him reign.
lessons.jesus: Early on resurrection morning, the angel gave the women a message from the risen Lord: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). Of all the disciples, Peter—the one who had denied the Lord three times—was named specifically. The risen Lord did not want Peter drowning in self-blame; he wanted Peter to know: You are still mine.
lessons.pray: Gracious Lord, thank you for blotting out our transgressions and no longer remembering our sins. Help us stop picking up the sins you have already forgiven, and stop binding each other with the past. As you have forgiven us, help us forgive each other in the same way, and set out afresh together in grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, amen.
teach: Some people find it hard to forgive their spouse; others find it hardest to forgive themselves. A word that can't be taken back, a decision that hurt the family—though long since confessed to God, it keeps replaying in the heart. God says, “I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25). To blot out is like wiping a chalkboard clean. God has already wiped it clean, yet we often pick up the chalk and write it all out again in our hearts, over and over.

So-called “forgiving yourself” is not really pardoning yourself; it is believing and receiving that God has already pardoned you. If God says, “I forgive you,” but I say, “I don't forgive me,” I am putting my standard above God's—and that is actually a form of pride. True humility admits my wrong, admits that God's grace is greater than my wrong, and then stands up again with gratitude.

This week we've learned: those who are forgiven can forgive; forgiveness is not forgetting, not excusing, and not staying in danger; forgiveness is handing the debt to God; after forgiveness, trust takes time to rebuild; and finally, we must also receive God's forgiveness for ourselves. Paul sums it up: “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13). Christ is the standard of our forgiveness, and Christ is the strength for it, too.
q: Is there something God has already forgiven, yet I still won't let myself off for?
Are my standards for myself harsher than God's standards for me?
talk: Is there something from the past that you've always felt sorry about toward me? I want to tell you that I'm willing to hand it to God together with you.
Of everything we've learned about forgiveness this week, which sentence do you most want to remember?
acts: Write down one piece of self-blame you need to let go of, and give it to God
Say to yourself: “The Lord has already forgiven me.”
Memorize Colossians 3:13 together with your spouse
lessons.noon: “I will not remember your sins” — Lord, right now I receive your forgiveness and stop rewriting old sins.

mem.t: But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;

date.t: A Date for Two Ambassadors of Reconciliation
s: Find a quiet spot and take turns sharing: How did you come to know Jesus and be reconciled to God? What changed in your heart back then?
Looking back over these five weeks on “Conflict and Forgiveness,” each of you name one way you’ve seen the other grow in making peace.
Together, think of a relationship among your family or friends that needs reconciling, and write down one small thing you can do for them.
Hold hands and pray: “Lord, you made peace with us first. Please make our home an ambassador of reconciliation.”

lessons.title: God Made Peace with Us First
lessons.theme: While we were still enemies, God had already come toward us

v: For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

lessons.still: Be still and think back to the days before you knew the Lord, or when you had drifted far from him. You didn’t love him then, yet he already loved you. Tell him: “Lord, thank you for coming toward me before I ever turned back to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Only through the gospel can we become self-emptied. Jesus’ death dealt with both our sinful nature and our sinful acts; his resurrection gives us a new life that can love and forgive. When we catch ourselves thinking, “Why should I be the one to back down first?” we go back to the cross: in love, God stooped first. Our focus is on Jesus, not on whether our spouse deserves it.
lessons.jesus: The Pharisees and scribes grumbled about Jesus: “This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them” (Luke 15:2). They meant it as criticism, but it is actually the most beautiful description of Jesus. He didn’t wait for sinners to improve before sitting down beside them; he walked right up to their tables. This is what the gospel of reconciliation truly looks like.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for sending your Son to die for us while we were still your enemies. We didn’t deserve it, yet you came first to make peace with us. May this gospel be the spring that flows through our home every day, so that we stop waiting for the other to change first, and instead love first, just as you did. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Paul writes, “God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Notice the order. It isn’t that we clean up our act first and then God comes to love us. While we were still sinners, even “while we were enemies” (Romans 5:10), God sent his Son. The first step toward reconciliation was God’s. That is the most astonishing news in the whole Bible.

These past weeks we’ve learned to go and make peace first, to manage our anger, and to forgive one another. But if we treat these only as techniques, we will soon run out of strength. We need to go back to the source: we can take the first step toward reconciliation because God first reconciled us to himself. Think of a well. A well we dig on our own runs dry, but a well connected to an underground spring never stops flowing. The gospel is that underground spring.

Paul goes on: “much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life” (Romans 5:10). Jesus’ death dealt with the sin between us and God; Jesus’ resurrection gives us new life. In marriage we need more than forgiveness; we need the power of this new life to love someone who is sometimes hard to love. The gospel isn’t only about the day we first believed. It is the power for reconciliation in our home every single day.
q: Do I often assume, without realizing it, that my spouse has to “shape up” before I’m willing to draw close?
Remembering that God loved me first while I was still far from him, what does that say to me about how I face my spouse today?
talk: Share: How have you experienced God loving you first and making peace with you first?
In our home, where could we learn to “take the first step” the way God did?
acts: Write a one-sentence prayer thanking God for making peace with you first
Today, take the first step toward your spouse in one small thing
Memorize 2 Corinthians 5:18
lessons.noon: “while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” — Lord, right now I remember that you loved me first.

lessons.title: The Cross Made Peace
lessons.theme: The cross can tear down the invisible walls between husband and wife

v: and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross.
You, being in past times alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds,
yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him,

lessons.still: Picture a wall between you and your spouse. Maybe it’s low; maybe it’s high. There’s no need to rush to analyze how it got there. Simply tell the Lord: “Lord, you are the one who tears down walls. I give this wall to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Behind every wall is a “self” protecting itself: afraid of being hurt again, of losing out, of losing control. The way of the cross is the self-emptied way; Jesus gave up his own body and made peace. When we are willing to lay down our self-protection and let Jesus reign, the wall begins to fall, and two people can truly become one.
lessons.jesus: Jesus cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last. At that very moment, “The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom” (Mark 15:38). The curtain that separated people from God was torn from above: God himself opened the way. Jesus’ death was the moment the dividing wall came down.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you shed your blood on the cross and made peace. We bring every brick and every wall between us to you. Remove our self-protection and our hostility, and make us one in you. Let our home be a witness to your peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Paul says we were once “alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds” (Colossians 1:21). Alienation is like a high wall: people on either side can hear each other but can’t get across. The deepest alienation between people and God is caused by sin. But Paul continues: “yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death” (Colossians 1:22). The cross is the place where God tore down that wall with his own hands.

Walls go up in marriage too. An unresolved hurt adds one brick; a long stretch of silence adds another. Different upbringings, habits, and attitudes toward money can slowly become a wall. At first it’s low enough to step over, but brick by brick it rises, until two people living under one roof feel as if they live on opposite sides of a wall. What we need is not just smarter communication skills, but to come together before the Lord who has already torn down what divides us.

Paul says Christ made peace “through the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). The walls between husband and wife, too, come down only through the cross. Not by someone winning the argument, nor by someone giving in more, but by both coming to the cross and admitting we need grace. Picture two people walking from opposite sides of the wall toward the same cross: the closer they come to the cross, the closer they come to each other.
q: Is there a wall between my spouse and me that is getting higher? What brick has been added lately?
In what areas am I still using a “wall” to protect myself?
talk: If you used a picture to describe the distance between us, what would it be? (For example: a low wall, a little stream, a door left half open.)
Is there one “brick” we could take down together today?
acts: Write down one “brick” you want to take off the wall
Spend ten extra minutes talking with your spouse, phones away
Gently take your spouse’s hand today
lessons.noon: “having made peace through the blood of his cross” — Lord, right now please tear down the wall in my heart.

lessons.title: The Ministry Entrusted to Us
lessons.theme: Those whom God has reconciled are also given the ministry of reconciliation

v: But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

lessons.still: Picture an ambassador standing on foreign soil; every word he speaks represents his country. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, in my home, am I your ambassador?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The ministry of reconciliation is practiced first at home: we are first reconciled to God (life), then husband and wife are reconciled to each other (relationships), and only then can we be ambassadors of reconciliation to others (ministry). Change begins with me, and the mission of reconciliation begins in my home.
lessons.jesus: When the risen Jesus appeared to his disciples, his first words were “Peace be to you.” Then he said, “As the Father has sent me, even so I send you” (John 20:21). The very disciples who had run away were forgiven and immediately sent out. Jesus entrusted the mission of reconciliation to people who had been reconciled.
lessons.pray: God who gives us the ministry of reconciliation, thank you for making us new creations and for not counting our trespasses against us. Help us stop keeping score at home and learn to forgive as you do. Make our marriage an embassy of Christ, where people can see your reconciliation and peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Paul says, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). In Christ, we are no longer defined by our past. Then he says God “reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). Those who have been reconciled have also been given a job: to be messengers of reconciliation.

Paul adds that God was “not reckoning to them their trespasses” (2 Corinthians 5:19). This is the very heart of reconciliation: God doesn’t keep score. In marriage, ambassadors of reconciliation learn to stop entering their spouse’s offenses in the ledger one by one. The more we drag up old accounts, the further away reconciliation gets. When we follow God’s example and stop counting our spouse’s trespasses against them, our home gains room for a fresh start.

“We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20). What matters most about an ambassador is not who he is, but whom he represents. At home, we represent Christ; before family and friends, our marriage represents Christ too. A couple who keeps on reconciling is itself a living sermon, showing people that the gospel really can enable two imperfect people to live out a perfect love.
q: In our marriage, am I still “keeping accounts” on my spouse? What shows up most often in my ledger?
If I am Christ’s ambassador in my home, what did my words and attitude today say about him?
talk: What do you think our marriage “represents” in the eyes of family and friends? What would we like it to represent?
Is there an old account we could decide together today to “no longer count against” each other?
acts: Choose one old account never to bring up again, and hand it over to God
Speak a blessing to your spouse that represents Christ
Pray for a friend or relative who needs to be reconciled to God
lessons.noon: “We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ” — Lord, right now let me represent your love in my home.

lessons.title: Put That to My Account
lessons.theme: Christ paid our debt, and we learn to carry burdens for each other

v: For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever,
no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.

lessons.still: Picture someone coming to you with a bill for an amount you could never repay in a lifetime. Then someone else walks over, takes the bill, and says, “Put it under my name.” Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for paying it all for me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled person says, “Whoever owes it pays for it. Not my problem.” The self-emptied person, like Paul and even more like Christ, is willing to say, “Put it on my account.” People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than gains and losses. When husband and wife are both willing to carry a little more for each other, home changes from a place of keeping accounts into a place where grace flows.
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ last words on the cross were “It is finished!” (John 19:30). In the original language this is a single word, meaning that a task has been completely accomplished. The debt we owed God, he carried in full on the cross; we no longer have to repay it. We can be reconciled with each other because Jesus first paid the full price for us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for putting all our debts to your account and paying them off with your own life. Take away our habit of keeping score in our hearts, and give us the burden-bearing love of Paul, and even more, your love. May our home no longer be a place of calculating gains and losses, but a place where grace flows. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Onesimus had been a slave in Philemon’s household. He left his master, and may also have owed him something. Later, while with Paul, he came to faith. Paul wrote to Philemon asking him to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). A broken relationship, even one weighed down with debt, found a whole new possibility through the gospel.

The most moving line is this: “if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account” (Philemon 1:18). Paul was willing to take on Onesimus’ debt so the two of them could be reconciled. This is the gospel in miniature: we owe God a debt we can never repay, yet Christ says, “Put that to my account.” Reconciliation is possible because someone paid the price.

In marriage, we too can learn this love that carries the other’s burden. When our spouse’s weakness costs us something, we don’t rush to settle the score; we say, “We’ll carry this one together.” When our spouse has wronged family or friends, we are willing to go with them to face it and make it right. Of course, carrying a burden does not mean covering up our spouse’s sin or tolerating harm. It means, in the truth, using love to mend the breach together.
q: Am I constantly “keeping accounts” with my spouse in my heart: who gives more, who owes more?
When I think of Christ putting all my debt to his account, what new perspective does that give me on what my spouse owes me?
talk: Was there a time when you felt I “carried” something for you, and it touched you deeply?
Is there anything lately about which we can say to each other, “We’ll carry this one together”?
acts: Today, close one “account” you’ve been keeping in your heart
Take on one task that normally belongs to your spouse
Pray a blessing over someone who once wronged you
lessons.noon: “put that to my account” — Lord, thank you for putting my debt to your account.

lessons.title: A Home That Makes Peace
lessons.theme: A reconciled couple becomes a home that helps others reconcile

v: I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.
Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

lessons.still: Think about your extended family, your church, or your friends. Is there a broken relationship that grieves you? Gently place those names before the Lord and say: “Lord, please use our home as an instrument of reconciliation.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: We build a household that belongs to God not only so that we ourselves can do well, but so that our home can become an instrument of reconciliation. The 920 life lets every “2” connected to me experience reconciliation; 235 teamwork lets husband and wife become spiritual comrades-in-arms together, passing on the gospel of reconciliation in our extended family and church.
lessons.jesus: Among the twelve disciples Jesus chose were Matthew, who had collected taxes for Rome, and “Simon who was called the Zealot” (Luke 6:15), from a movement that resisted Rome. These two might well have been enemies, yet at Jesus’ side they became companions. Jesus shows us that his presence can turn people set against each other into one family.
lessons.pray: God who reconciles, thank you for leading us these five weeks to learn to face conflict, manage our anger, forgive each other, and be reconciled anew in the gospel. Make our home a peacemaking home that carries your peace into our extended family, our church, and our community. And please protect every family living in danger, and lead them to find help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Two women in the Philippian church who had served together fell out with each other. Paul wrote, “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). He didn’t take sides; he brought both of them back to being “in the Lord.” Then he asked his “true partner” (Philippians 4:3) to help them. This gives us two reminders: reconciliation requires returning to the Lord, and sometimes it also needs a trusted third person to help.

Paul also says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). “As much as it is up to you” means we take the initiative and put our hearts into it; “if it is possible” also admits that sometimes reconciliation doesn’t depend on us alone. If the other person keeps hurting us and refuses to change, or if there is violence or threats, we can still forgive and pray for them, but we do not have to force ourselves to stay in danger. Seeking help from a pastor and from professionals is exactly the kind of help a “true partner” gives.

Over these five weeks we have learned that conflict comes from self on the throne in our hearts; the five steps to reconcile (Stop · See · Own · Ask · Act) when we go to make peace first; how to be angry without sinning; how to forgive seventy times seven; and the foundation beneath it all: God first reconciled us to himself in Christ. A home that keeps on reconciling is like a lamp, shining on the broken relationships around it. A reconciled couple can become that gentle “true partner” in someone else’s home, walking with them toward reconciliation.
q: Looking back on these five weeks of “Conflict and Forgiveness,” what has been my own biggest change?
In my circle of life, who needs a “true partner” to walk with them toward reconciliation?
talk: Over these five weeks, what growth in making peace have you seen in me? Please give one specific example.

How could our home help others reconcile? For example, through hospitality, walking alongside them, or praying together for a particular relationship. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one person you’d like to walk alongside.)
acts: Pray together for a relationship that needs reconciling
Write a card to encourage a friend who is going through conflict
Tell your spouse the one thing from these five weeks you’re most thankful for
lessons.noon: “to think the same way in the Lord” — Lord, right now make us people who bring peace.

mem.t: subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

date.t: A Date Where You Take Turns Leading
s: Split the date into two halves: one of you plans the first half, the other plans the second. When it’s the other’s turn, happily follow along.
During the date, take turns answering: “When have I recently made you feel respected and heard?”
Think together of a family decision coming up soon, and practice both listening fully to each other’s thoughts before deciding together.
Finally, bow your heads together and pray: “Lord Jesus, you are the Commander of our home. Together we submit to you.”

lessons.title: The Overarching Principle: Submit to One Another
lessons.theme: A Spirit-filled home naturally overflows with mutual submission

v: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father;
subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

lessons.still: Be still and ask the Holy Spirit to fill you. Consider the word “submission.” What does it stir in your heart: peace, resistance, or pain? Whatever it is, bring it honestly to the Lord and say: “Lord, teach me what submission means in your heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When the self-ruled person hears “submit,” the first reaction is “Why me?” or “You should submit to me!” Both are grabs for power. The self-emptied person first asks, “Lord, how can I let you reign?” When both let Jesus reign, mutual submission is no longer oppression but freedom; no longer losing, but a win for both.
lessons.jesus: At twelve years old, Jesus talked with the teachers in the temple, and even they were amazed. Yet afterward “he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). The Son of God willingly submitted to his earthly parents. Jesus shows us that submission is not a sign of inadequacy but a choice of love.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, fill us, and fill our home with songs, thanksgiving, and mutual submission. We confess that we often want to grab control and make the other fit in with us. Teach us to submit to one another in reverence for Christ, to build each other up in you, and to make our home a place where you reign. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: When it comes to submission in marriage, many people jump straight to “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). But in the verse just before, Paul states the overarching principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). In some of the oldest Greek manuscripts, verse 22 has no verb of its own; “be subject” is carried over from verse 21. In other words, everything Paul teaches husbands and wives sits within the larger frame of submitting to one another.

This passage begins with “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18) and goes on to describe what being Spirit-filled looks like: speaking to one another in psalms and songs, making melody in our hearts, giving thanks for all things, and submitting to one another. Submission isn’t forced out of us; it is the fruit of being filled with the Spirit. Think of two people paddling a small boat. It isn’t one person straining while the other is dragged along; the boat moves forward smoothly only when both pay attention to each other’s rhythm.

The words “one another” matter enormously. Submission is not a one-way demand but a two-way attitude: I am willing to put your needs ahead of my preferences, and you are willing to do the same for me. It isn’t a power game with a winner and a loser; it is two people bowing together under Christ, then building each other up out of Christ’s love. The coming weeks on the roles of husbands and wives all start from here.
q: What feeling does the word “submission” first stir in me? Where does that feeling come from?
Do I more often demand that my spouse submit to me, or do I more often take the initiative to submit to my spouse?
talk: In our home, where do you feel we are already “submitting to one another”? Please give a specific example.

Is there something lately where you’d like me to listen more to your thoughts? Please say it gently. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one area where you’d like to submit to them first.)
acts: Today, in one small thing, take the initiative to do it your spouse’s way
Before making a decision, first ask: “What do you think?”
Memorize Ephesians 5:21
lessons.noon: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” — Lord, right now I choose to revere you and let you reign.

lessons.title: Submission That Comes from Strength
lessons.theme: True submission flows from strength and identity, not from weakness

v: He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear,
though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus praying in tears in the Garden of Gethsemane. He told the Father his most honest feelings, and then he said “yes.” Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, put your heart within me, so that my submission flows from love, not from fear.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride leaves its rightful place and grabs for power; humility lets go of power and returns to our rightful place. Jesus modeled the most complete humility: he was the Son, yet he willingly obeyed. When husband and wife both take on the mind of Christ, they stop fighting over who is in charge and instead let Jesus be in charge together. Humility inspires humility, and the home is revived.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). Jesus’ obedience was not cold compliance but joy in close fellowship with the Father. The root of submission is knowing we are loved and never alone.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, though you were the Son, you willingly learned obedience. We confess that we often clutch our rights, afraid of losing out or being looked down on. Make our identity secure in your love, so that we freely build each other up in love, and our home displays the beauty of your humility. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Hebrews says of Jesus, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). Notice “though he was a Son”: obedience took nothing away from his identity as the Son. Jesus knew clearly who he was, where he had come from, and where he was going, and so he could submit willingly. This is the key to understanding submission: Christlike submission does not come from powerlessness or low self-worth, but from a secure identity and from love.

Many people assume that the one who submits is the lesser person. But the Son of God’s submission did not make him any less the Son of God. In the same way, a spouse who submits in marriage loses none of their worth. Think of a brilliant pianist accompanying a singer. He sets aside the chance to play solo not because his skill falls short, but because he wants to bring a more beautiful song to life.

The passage also says Jesus offered prayers “with strong crying and tears” and was heard “for his godly fear” (Hebrews 5:7). Jesus’ obedience was not suppressing himself to comply; it was a choice he freely made after bringing his real feelings to the Father. True submission comes from freedom. Forced compliance isn’t submission; it is mere capitulation. In marriage, too, we can express our feelings honestly, and then freely choose to build each other up in love.
q: Do I associate submission with being “worth less”? Where did that idea come from?
In our home, what “right” am I clutching tightly and refusing to let go of?
talk: In what ways do you feel I’m like an “accompanying pianist,” willing to help you shine?
Is there something where you hope we could both lay down our own insistence and seek Christ’s will together?
acts: Write down one “right” you want to let go of
Today, “accompany” your spouse once by helping their plan succeed
Read Hebrews 5:7–9 and meditate on Christ’s obedience
lessons.noon: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” — Lord, right now let my submission flow from love.

lessons.title: Not Lording It Over, but Working for Joy
lessons.theme: Authority exists to help the other person’s joy, not to control them

v: We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy. For you stand firm in faith.
not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.

lessons.still: Recall a small scene at home today: Who was doing the housework? Who was making the decisions? Whose voice was heard most often? Without judging, just look quietly, and then tell the Lord: “Lord, let me see what I am like at home.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Lording it over” is self on the throne: I want you to do it my way. “Working for your joy” is the self-emptied life: I’m willing to serve you according to your needs. The order of relationships is God, self, others, things. People matter more than tasks; don’t wound the people we love for the sake of controlling things.
lessons.jesus: A Gentile woman came to Jesus pleading for her daughter, who was possessed by a demon. Her reply was full of humility and faith. Hearing it, Jesus said to her, “For this saying, go your way. The demon has gone out of your daughter” (Mark 7:29). Jesus truly listened to a woman’s words and responded to her need. He shows us that respect and listening are themselves a service of love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve. Forgive us for using power, volume, or emotions to lord it over each other at home. Help us learn your servant’s way, respecting each other in matters great and small and working for each other’s joy, so that our home lives out the life of your kingdom. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Paul was an apostle with spiritual authority, yet he told the Corinthian church, “We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:24). Peter also reminded the church’s elders to lead “not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). In God’s household, no authority or responsibility exists to crush people; it exists to build them up.

Marriage is the same. No role or responsibility is a license to control the other person; it is a call to serve them. If anyone uses the verses about “head” or “submission” to control their spouse, demanding unconditional obedience and forbidding them to voice an opinion, that is “lording it over,” not “working for their joy,” and it has strayed from the heart of Scripture. In a household that belongs to God, the question is not “Who gets the final say?” but “How can I help you be more joyful and more like Christ?”

What does mutual submission look like in daily life? It is listening fully to the other’s thoughts before making a decision; being willing to set aside your own preferences, such as weekend plans or what to have for dinner; respecting the other’s feelings and opinions, even when you don’t end up doing exactly what they suggest; and stepping in to share the load when the other is tired. It is like two people dancing together: one isn’t dragging the other along; each pays attention and responds to the other.
q: In our home, are there areas where I “lord it over” my spouse rather than helping them?
When was the last time I set aside my own preference so that my spouse could flourish?
talk: In our home, when do you feel most respected? When do you feel your voice hasn’t been heard?
Could we make a small agreement together to “hear each other out completely before deciding”?
acts: Today, set aside a preference in one thing so your spouse can flourish
Before a decision, hear your spouse out completely
Take on a household chore your spouse usually does
lessons.noon: “We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy” — Lord, right now make me someone who helps my spouse’s joy.

lessons.title: Submission Never Includes Violence
lessons.theme: Submission is freely given love in the Lord, never enduring violence and control

v: But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.
When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him,
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.

lessons.still: Take a slow, deep breath and sense God’s presence. You were created in God’s image, and you are precious beyond measure in his eyes. Tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for valuing me. Please protect every person in our home.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Control and violence are the most extreme form of self on the throne: one person sits on the throne and makes another live by his or her will. This is taking God’s place and trampling on God’s image. Letting Jesus reign means acknowledging that my spouse belongs to God, not to me. In Christ, no one has the right to harm another person.
lessons.jesus: In the end Jesus went to the cross, willingly laying down his life to redeem the world; that was a mission unlike any other. But before that, when people tried to harm him, he slipped away many times. For example: “They sought again to seize him, and he went out of their hand” (John 10:39). Jesus does not ask us to remain in violence.
lessons.pray: Lord, our protector, you see every person as precious. Heal the hearts that have been wounded at home. Protect all who are in danger, lead them to a safe place, and bring them to people willing to help. Shine your light on us as well: if there is any control or harm in us, lead us to repent and turn to you. May our home be a safe home. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: The motive for mutual submission is “the fear of Christ,” so submission always stays under Christ’s authority. When human demands went against God’s will, the apostles said, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). God has never asked anyone to submit to evil. Anyone who demands that their spouse join them in lying or sinning, or demands that they put up with harm, has already crossed the boundary of submission.

We must say this clearly: physical violence (pushing, hitting, choking, smashing things to intimidate), verbal violence (humiliation, intimidation, threats), sexual coercion, financial control, monitoring someone’s whereabouts or phone, and cutting them off from family and friends are not things submission can ever cover. They are sins against God that harm the image of God. Submission never includes enduring violence or control of any kind. In Scripture, when people plotted to kill Paul, “his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket” (Acts 9:25). Escaping violence is wisdom, not weakness, and certainly not betrayal.

If you feel afraid at home, please remember: safety comes first. Tell someone you trust, contact your pastor, and seek professional help from social workers or counselors; if you are in immediate danger, call the police right away. Leaving for a safe place does not mean giving up on your marriage, nor is it disobeying God. The church, too, should protect those who are hurt. If you realize you are the one using anger, threats, or money to control your spouse, Jesus calls you to repent as well, and to actively seek professional help.
q: Have I ever misunderstood “submission,” thinking I must put up with everything?
In my words or attitude, is there anything that makes my spouse feel afraid or controlled?
talk: In our home, do you feel free to express a different opinion, even to say “no”?
How can we help each other feel safe and respected at home? (If you feel afraid at home, please don’t push yourself into this conversation; first talk with a pastor or professional you trust.)
acts: Save the contact details of a pastor or counselor you trust
Pray for people living with domestic violence
Tell your spouse: “You can safely say no to me.”
lessons.noon: “We must obey God rather than men” — Lord, right now make our home a safe home.

lessons.title: Bowing Together Before the Commander
lessons.theme: The foundation of mutual submission is both of us submitting to Christ

v: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?”
He said, “No; but I have come now as commander of the LORD’s army.” Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, “What does my lord say to his servant?”
The prince of the LORD’s army said to Joshua, “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy.” Joshua did so.

lessons.still: Picture the two of you standing side by side before the Lord of glory. You are no longer arguing about who is right; you are both bowing your heads. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, whatever you have to say, tell us.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Three foundations: Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. When husband and wife both center their lives on these three, they stop fighting over who reigns and instead let Jesus reign together. The goal of mutual submission is to let Jesus receive all the glory together and to build a household that belongs to God.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30). On earth, the Son of God put the Father’s will above his own. When husband and wife both learn to pray this way, it is no longer a tug-of-war over who submits to whom, but two people submitting together to the Father’s will.
lessons.pray: Commander of the LORD’s army, we bow together before you. We no longer ask you to take anyone’s side; we only ask that both of us stand on your side. Be the Commander of our home. Teach us to submit to one another in reverence for you, to build each other up in love, and together to let you receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
teach: Before attacking Jericho, Joshua saw a man with a drawn sword in his hand. Joshua asked, “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” He answered, “No; but I have come now as commander of the LORD’s army” (Joshua 5:13–14). Many interpreters believe this was an appearance of Christ before his incarnation. The answer is surprising: the Lord had not come to take anyone’s side; he had come to take command.

When couples fight, they often ask God in prayer, “Are you on my side or on theirs?” The Commander’s answer reminds us that the question is not whose side God is on, but whether we are on God’s side. Joshua immediately “fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:14). When husband and wife both bow before the Commander, mutual submission gains a shared center.

This week we have learned that mutual submission is the fruit of being filled with the Spirit; that true submission comes from the heart of Christ and is freely given love; that in the Lord’s household, power is for serving, not for lording it over others; and that submission never includes enduring violence or control. In the end, everything comes back to this: two people submitting to Christ together. The next two weeks, on the callings of husbands and wives, both start from this place of bowing low.
q: In my prayers, do I often want God to be “on my side”?
If Christ is the Commander of our home, what might he be telling me to do today?
talk: Has this week’s study of “submission” changed how you used to see it? Please share one specific point.
How can we “bow down” together? For example, when we disagree, we could first pray together and ask the Lord what he wants.
acts: When you disagree, pray together first, then talk it through
Say together with your spouse: “Lord, whatever you have to say, tell us.”
Write down one thing in which you will submit to God together
lessons.noon: “What does my lord say to his servant?” — Lord, right now we bow together to hear what you say.

mem.t: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,

date.t: An Evening He Plans for You
s: The husband is in charge of this date: prepare a drink or snack your wife enjoys, and put both phones aside.
The husband asks: “This week, how did I love you in a way that made you feel most cherished?” Then he listens quietly to the end, without defending or explaining.
The wife places her hand on her husband’s shoulder and prays for him: that the Lord would help him love and lead this family the way Christ does.
The husband prays for his wife using Ephesians 5:25, and names one thing he is willing to give up for her this month.

lessons.title: The Head Is the One Who Goes First
lessons.theme: Being the head means not sitting above, but going ahead and carrying the load

v: For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.
Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Be still and place the word “head” before the Lord. Husbands, ask him: “Lord, in your eyes, what does being the head look like?” Wives, ask the Lord for a heart that prays for your husband rather than grading him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled husband treats “head” as a throne and expects the family to revolve around him; the self-emptied husband treats “head” as a cross and lays himself down for his family first. Only when a husband first submits to Christ his Head and lets Jesus reign will he stop trying to take God’s place, and only then can he lead his family toward Christ.
lessons.jesus: When soldiers came with swords and clubs to arrest Jesus, he stepped forward and said, “If therefore you seek me, let these go their way” (John 18:8). When danger came, he stood at the very front so that his disciples could get away. This is what being the head looks like: not hiding behind the family and barking orders, but standing in front of them to face the storm.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the head of the church and the Savior who laid down his life. Remove the pride in our hearts that wants to be king and to be in control. Help husbands learn to go first in serving, and help wives learn to uphold their husbands in prayer. May there be only one true King in our home: you. Amen.
teach: This week’s passages are addressed to husbands. Wives, please don’t use them to measure your husband; use them to pray for him, just as next week’s passages for wives are not for husbands to demand of their wives. Paul says, “the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly” (Ephesians 5:23); “assembly” is the WEB’s word for the church. When many people hear “head,” they think of a boss, a commander, the one who gets the final say. But Paul immediately adds, “being himself the savior of the body” (Ephesians 5:23). Christ’s way of being head is to save, not to order people around.

Jesus himself defined what it means to be first. He said that the rulers of the nations “lord it over them,” and then: “But it shall not be so among you” (Mark 10:43). In God’s kingdom, “Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all” (Mark 10:44). Picture a mountaineering team. The person in front doesn’t have the easiest job; he clears the trail, scouts the route, and is the first to step into danger. A husband who is the head goes first in the home: first to admit he’s wrong, first to pray, first to take responsibility, first to serve.

The overarching principle of this passage is “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21). A husband’s headship is service, accountable to Christ, within the frame of mutual submission; it is not unrestrained authority. For “the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). So the question a husband asks is not “Did she listen to me?” but “Did I serve her the way Jesus does?” The authority of the head is for blessing, not for control.
q: Husbands: In what area of our home do I often want to “have the final say,” yet rarely “go first” to carry the load?
Wives: Have I ever used the word “head” to make demands of my husband or criticize him? How can I turn that into prayer for him today?
talk: Wife first: Recall a time you felt your husband “went first” and carried a load for our family. What was it? Then husband: What was going on in your heart at that time?

In our home, is there one area where you wish we were more like a mountaineering team, with someone clearing the trail and everyone looking out for each other? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to them.)
acts: Husbands: Today, take on a household task that no one wants to do
Wives: Pray for your husband: “Lord, make him a servant leader”
Read Mark 10:45 together, and each name one way to serve the other
lessons.noon: “the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” — Lord Jesus, right now teach me to serve first at home instead of waiting to be served.

lessons.title: Giving Himself Up for Her: The Direction of Love
lessons.theme: Christ’s love gives first and offers itself for the other’s good

v: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word,
that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without defect.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

lessons.still: Think of Jesus on the cross: when he gave himself up for you, you hadn’t yet become any better. Quietly receive this love. Husbands, ask the Lord to let this love flow from you to your wife; wives, ask the Lord to let your husband first deeply experience being loved by Christ.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-ruled love asks, “What can you give me?” Self-emptied love asks, “What can I give up for you?” A husband’s strength to love his wife doesn’t come from gritting his teeth, but from first being filled with Christ’s self-giving love. Through the gospel, the old self-centered life is crucified, and the new life naturally pours out self-giving love.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Not long after saying it, he really did go to the cross. Jesus’ love was not a declaration that stayed on his lips, but action that paid a price. A husband’s love is the same: love is a verb, and it often costs something.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you gave yourself up for us, and so we have life. Fill husbands with your love, so that they give not grudgingly but gladly; and let wives become more like you as they are loved. May our home be a witness to your glory. Amen.
teach: Paul’s command to husbands has just one core verb: “love.” And the standard of that love is astonishingly high: “even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). In that society, asking wives to submit was nothing unusual; what was truly shocking was what Paul asked of husbands. It isn’t that your wife must first deserve your love; like Christ, you love first, even when she isn’t being lovable.

Christ’s love has a direction. He gave himself up “that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:26). A husband’s love has a direction too: helping his wife grow and shine in the Lord. Picture a gardener caring for a rose. He doesn’t spend every day complaining that the flower isn’t red enough; he waters, feeds, and shields it from the wind so it can bloom more beautifully on its own. A husband is not his wife’s judge, but a companion walking with her as she is washed by God’s word and built up by God’s love.

Jesus said, “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). For most husbands, laying down your life doesn’t mean taking a bullet for her someday; it means laying down a little every day: putting down your phone to hear about her day; laying down “I’m right” and saying sorry first; giving up your weekend plans to go with her to visit her parents. These small deaths are Christ’s love lived out at home. God’s purpose is to “present the assembly to himself gloriously” (Ephesians 5:27), and also to give us a home that shines with love.
q: Husbands: What have I been reluctant to give up for my wife lately: time, pride, or habits?
Wives: How can I pray specifically for my husband, asking the Lord to let him first experience being loved by Christ?
talk: Lately, what small thing made you feel, “He gave something up for me”? Please be specific.
Wife shares: If there were one thing that could help you be freer and shine more in the Lord, how would you like your husband to walk with you in it?
acts: Husbands: Today, set aside something of your own to do what your wife wants to do
Wives: Pray for your husband: “Lord, let him experience your love every day”
Husbands: Ask your wife, “How can I help you today?”
lessons.noon: “even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her” — Lord, right now let your self-giving love flow through me to my family.

lessons.title: As Their Own Bodies
lessons.theme: To nourish and cherish is to notice her needs and care for her tenderly

v: Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself.
For no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly,
because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones.

lessons.still: Place your hand over your heart and think about how you take care of yourself when you’re tired or hurting. Then quietly ask: “Lord, do I pay the same attention to my spouse’s tiredness and needs?” Ask the Holy Spirit to open our eyes.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled person is very sensitive to his own pain and very slow to notice others’ pain. The self-emptied husband treats his wife’s needs as his own, because we are one. When we live from the heart by the Spirit, we will see her; when we live from the head by ourselves, we only calculate who is giving more.
lessons.jesus: The disciples were so busy serving that they had no time even to eat, and Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile” (Mark 6:31). He saw how tired they were and made arrangements for them to rest. Jesus’ leadership included cherishing: he didn’t just assign work; he cared about the bodies and souls of those who followed him.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for feeding and protecting us every day with Christ’s love. Give husbands a sensitive, tender heart to notice their wives’ tiredness and care for them as they care for their own bodies; and make wives willing to open up and give their husbands the chance to love them. Help us truly live out our life as one. Amen.
teach: Paul uses a picture everyone understands: “no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29). When we cut a finger, we don’t scold it for being careless; we immediately stop the bleeding and bandage it. Since husband and wife are one, “He who loves his own wife loves himself” (Ephesians 5:28). Hurting your wife is hurting your own body; neglecting her is neglecting your own wound.

In the original, to “nourish” carries the sense of feeding and sustaining; to “cherish” means to give warmth and treasure tenderly. Paul uses the same word for a mother caring for her children: “like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). A husband’s love is not only about providing for the family; it also nourishes her soul and gives her warmth. What many wives lack is not money, but a simple “Thank you for all you do,” a cup of hot tea, or an evening when someone is willing to listen to her.

Paul says Christ treats the church this way, “because we are members of his body” (Ephesians 5:30). Christ never despises the church for its weakness; every day he feeds, protects, and heals. A husband’s nourishing and cherishing calls for careful attention: Is she sleeping well lately? What is stressing her? When she says “I’m fine,” is something actually wrong? A man who knows how to care for his own body can also learn to care for his wife in body, mind, and spirit.
q: Husbands: Am I as sensitive to my wife’s tiredness as I am to my own wounds, or do I usually only find out when she tells me?
Wives: Am I willing to let my husband see my needs, rather than just saying “I’m fine”? How can I pray for his sensitivity?
talk: In this season, where do you most need to be cared for: physically, emotionally, or spiritually?
Husband asks wife: “What kind of care makes you feel most cherished?” Wife, please give a specific example. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one need you’ve noticed in them.)
acts: Husbands: Make your wife a hot drink and ask whether she’s tired today
Wives: Pray for your husband: “Lord, give him a sensitive, cherishing heart”
Each name one area where you need care right now
lessons.noon: “no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” — Lord, right now let me cherish my spouse as I care for myself.

lessons.title: Live with Understanding; Never Be Harsh
lessons.theme: Know her and honor her: headship is never control

v: You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered.
Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them.

lessons.still: Be still, and before the Lord look honestly at your tone, your eyes, and your hands. Ask him: “Lord, is anyone in my home afraid because of me?” If you yourself are living in fear, tell the Lord about that fear too. He sees you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Control is the most hidden form of pride: wanting others to live by my will is wanting to take God’s place. A true head first returns to his rightful place and submits to Christ, and honors his wife as someone God created who shares the grace of life with him. Let people be people, and let God be God; only then will home be a safe place.
lessons.jesus: A woman who had suffered from bleeding touched Jesus’ clothes. Trembling, she fell down before him and “told him all the truth” (Mark 5:33). In the middle of a pressing crowd, Jesus stopped, listened to her whole story, and called her “Daughter.” Jesus valued the dignity of every woman and was willing to take time to understand her pain. That is exactly what living “according to knowledge” looks like.
lessons.pray: Lord, you value the dignity of every person. Help husbands live with their wives according to knowledge, understanding them, honoring them, and never treating them harshly. Wherever there is control, intimidation, or harm, shine your light, break its hold, and lead us to seek help. Protect those who are suffering at home, and bring them safety and healing. Amen.
teach: Peter says, “You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge” (1 Peter 3:7). Living “according to knowledge” means making the effort to understand her: her temperament, her pressures, her rhythms. Picture a good doctor; he wouldn’t prescribe medicine without reading the patient’s chart. Many husbands love their wives, but in the way they themselves want to be loved. Living according to knowledge means understanding her first, then loving her.

When Peter calls the wife “the weaker vessel,” he means that women of that time were more easily harmed, physically and socially, not that her worth is lower; for husband and wife are “joint heirs of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7).
