That is why husbands are to give her honor. Peter adds a sobering line: live this way “that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3:7). God ties how a husband treats his wife to his own relationship with God.

Paul also says, “Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them” (Colossians 3:19), that is, never treat them harshly. We must be clear: the authority of the head never includes control or harm. Hitting and shoving, intimidation and verbal abuse, forced sex, withholding money, restricting her contact with family and friends, monitoring her whereabouts: these are violence and control. They are sin, not biblical headship. If a wife is living in this, submission does not mean staying in danger, and forgiveness does not mean continuing to endure it. Safety comes first: please seek help from a trusted pastor and professional agencies, and in an emergency call the police. If a husband realizes he is doing these things, asking for help is the first step of repentance.
q: Husbands: Have my words, tone, or decisions ever made my wife feel afraid or disrespected? Am I willing to admit it to God and to her?
Wives: How can I pray for my husband, asking the Lord to help him understand and honor me more? If I don’t feel safe, whom can I turn to for help first?
talk: What part of you would you most like me to understand better: your pressures, your dreams, or your daily rhythms?

Is there a way of talking or an atmosphere in our home that makes you tense? How can we change it together? (If discussing this would make you feel unsafe, please don’t; contact a pastor or counselor instead.)
acts: Husbands: Ask your wife one question to get to know her better, and listen quietly to the end
Wives: Pray for your husband: “Lord, help him live with me in understanding and honor”
Save the contact details of a pastor or counseling service you trust
lessons.noon: “giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life” — Lord, right now let me honor the one who shares your grace with me.

lessons.title: Leadership That Stoops Low
lessons.theme: A husband leads by stooping to serve and kneeling to pray, every day

v: So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus with a towel around his waist, kneeling in front of you to wash your feet. Don’t rush to refuse; let him serve you first. Then quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, today at home, for whom can I stoop low?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change begins with me. A husband doesn’t have to wait for his wife to submit before he loves her, just as Jesus didn’t wait for the disciples to improve before washing their feet. Pride provokes pride; humility inspires humility. A husband who is willing to stoop low will often bring about a softer home.
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew Peter was about to fall, and he told him, “but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail” (Luke 22:32). Jesus didn’t only serve the disciples’ needs; he also interceded for them in their weakest moments. A husband’s spiritual leadership also begins with praying for his wife.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are Lord, yet you washed your disciples’ feet. Help husbands tie on your towel, going first to serve and taking the lead in prayer at home; and help wives uphold their husbands in prayer every day. May we not only know, but do, so that your glory is revealed in our home. Amen.
teach: At the Last Supper, after Jesus had washed the disciples’ feet, he asked them, “Do you know what I have done to you?” Then he said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). Jesus did not stop being Lord, but the way he was Lord was to stoop down. This week we have seen that, for a husband, being the head means tying this towel around his own waist.

Washing feet was a servant’s job back then, dirty and lowly. A husband’s “foot washing” might be taking over the housework when she’s sick; not dragging up old wrongs when she says something wrong; praising her in front of family and friends; taking the lead spiritually by saying, “Let’s pray together.” Jesus said, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). The blessing is not in knowing, but in doing. A husband’s spiritual leadership is not preaching at his wife, but doing it himself first.

Wives, how can you pray for your husband? You can use this week’s five pictures: ask the Lord to help him go first like a servant; to experience Christ’s love so he can give himself up; to have a sensitive, cherishing heart; to live with you according to knowledge, free from all anger and control; and to be willing to stoop low every day. Praying for your husband is more powerful than reminding him, because it is the Holy Spirit who changes hearts. Husbands, remember too: the first responsibility of the head is to kneel and pray for his family.
q: Husbands: What “stooping-low” service at home have I always felt shouldn’t be my job?
Wives: Of this week’s five pictures for praying for my husband, which one do I most want to keep praying for him?
talk: This week, in what did you sense me learning to serve you the way Jesus does?
How can we build the habit of “praying one sentence for each other every day”? Think of a specific time or way.
acts: Husbands: Today, take the initiative to say, “Let’s pray together”
Wives: Use this week’s five pictures to pray one sentence each for your husband
Do one small act of “foot-washing” service for your spouse
lessons.noon: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” — Lord, right now I am willing to stoop low and serve as you did.

43.title: Wives: Building the Home with Wisdom

mem.t: Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.

date.t: Laying a Good Brick for Our Home
s: Walk around your home together. In each corner, name one thing that happened there that you’re thankful for.
The husband puts the heart of Proverbs 31:29 into his own words: “In my eyes, the most precious thing about you is…”
The wife shares a dream or a burden on her heart, and the husband just listens, without rushing to give advice.
The husband places his hand on his wife’s shoulder and prays for her, asking the Lord to give her wisdom, peace, and joy.

lessons.title: What Submission Is, and What It Is Not
lessons.theme: Submission is a free response in the Lord, not blind obedience

v: Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.
But as the assembly is subject to Christ, so let the wives also be to their own husbands in everything.
Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

lessons.still: Be still and honestly place the word “submission” before the Lord. Perhaps it brings you warmth; perhaps it brings you pain. Tell the Lord: “Lord, teach me the true meaning of submission through your word, not through people’s words.” Husbands, ask the Lord to make you someone worthy of trust.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The opposite of submission is not expressing an opinion; it is self on the throne, insisting on being in charge of everything. And the opposite of control is not weakness, but the self-emptied life. True submission begins by letting Jesus reign. A wife who first submits to the Lord won’t blindly follow people, nor does she need to fight anyone for power, because her security is in the Lord.
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). The Son is equal with the Father, yet he willingly submitted in the mission of redemption. Jesus shows us that submission is not about being inferior, nor about being forced; it is a free choice that flows from love and trust.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that you yourself first submitted to the Father and went to the cross for us. Help us all to submit to one another in reverence for you. Give wives a free and willing heart, and give husbands lives worthy of trust. Protect all who are hurting and afraid at home, and lead them to safety and help. Amen.
teach: This week’s passages are addressed to wives. Husbands, please don’t use them to make demands of your wife; use them to pray for her. Paul says, “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22). In the original Greek, this verse actually has no verb of its own; “be subject” carries over from the previous verse, “subjecting yourselves to one another.” In other words, a wife’s submission is part of the whole household’s mutual submission, not a requirement singled out and pressed onto one person alone.

Scripture never tells husbands to “make their wives submit”; it only invites wives to choose submission themselves. This shows that submission is a free response, offered willingly out of trust in the Lord, not something forced. The key lies in “as to the Lord” and “as is fitting in the Lord” (Colossians 3:18). Submission happens in the Lord, so it has limits: if a wife is asked to sin, deceive, or violate her conscience, she must remember, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). A submissive wife still has her own voice, gifts, and judgment.

We must also say this clearly: submission never means enduring violence. Physical harm, verbal abuse and intimidation, forced sex, financial control, being forbidden contact with family and friends: these are all sin, not biblical submission. Forgiveness does not mean staying in danger. If your safety or your family’s safety is threatened, safety comes first: please seek help from a trusted pastor, a professional counselor, or a social service agency, and in an emergency call the police. Leaving danger and seeking protection is not disobeying God.
q: Wives: When I hear “submission,” what rises in my heart: trust, fear, or resistance? Where do these feelings come from?
Husbands: Have I ever used “wives must submit” to override her opinion? How can I turn that into praying for her today?
talk: In our home, what kind of atmosphere makes it easier for you to trust the other’s lead?
What upcoming decision could we use to practice praying together first and hearing each other out before deciding together?
acts: Wives: In one small thing, gladly honor your husband’s suggestion
Husbands: Pray for your wife: “Lord, let her rest and be free in you”
Together, list one thing you need to decide jointly; pray first, then discuss it
lessons.noon: “as is fitting in the Lord” — Lord, right now I submit to you first, and then love my family in you.

lessons.title: A Gentle and Quiet Spirit
lessons.theme: The most beautiful adornment is a heart at rest before God

v: In the same way, wives, be in subjection to your own husbands, so that, even if any don’t obey the Word, they may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word,
seeing your pure behavior in fear.
Let your beauty come not from the outward adorning of braiding your hair, and of wearing gold ornaments or of putting on fine clothing,
but from the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in God’s sight.
For this is how in the past the holy women who hoped in God also adorned themselves, being in subjection to their own husbands.
So Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose children you now are if you do well and are not put in fear by any terror.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath, then slowly let it out. Picture a lake: when the wind stops, its surface clearly reflects the sky. Tell the Lord: “Lord, quiet my heart so that it reflects you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Anxiety and quarreling often come from my wanting to hold on to control, afraid that things won’t go my way. A gentle and quiet spirit hands control back to God: let God be God, and I no longer have to carry the whole household on my shoulders. When our focus is on Jesus, not on our husband or our circumstances, our hearts grow quiet.
lessons.jesus: The storm was raging and the disciples were panicking, yet Jesus was asleep in the stern. When he woke, he said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39). The peace within Jesus was greater than the storm outside. A gentle and quiet spirit doesn’t come from the absence of storms, but from having the Lord in the boat.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, calm the storms in our hearts. Give wives an enduring gentle and quiet spirit, not out of fear, but out of hope in you; and make husbands a source of stability in the home, not a storm. May our lives become an adornment that is very precious in your sight. Amen.
teach: Peter was writing to wives whose husbands did not yet believe. He told them they didn’t need to rely on preaching, for their husbands “may be won by the behavior of their wives without a word” (1 Peter 3:1). This is a great comfort for anyone using this course alone, whose spouse isn’t yet walking alongside them: the witness of a life is often more powerful than a hundred attempts at persuasion. Change begins with me, not with demanding that he change.

Peter says true beauty comes “from the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is very precious in God’s sight” (1 Peter 3:4). Quiet doesn’t mean never speaking, and gentle doesn’t mean having no personality. A quiet spirit is like a lake that is still clear after the storm has passed; gentleness is strength placed under the Lord’s control. Outward adornment fades, but inward adornment grows more beautiful with time.

It’s worth noticing that Peter goes on to say wives are Sarah’s children “if you do well and are not put in fear by any terror” (1 Peter 3:6). The gentleness and quietness Scripture speaks of is not trembling under threats, but the steadiness that comes from trusting God, like the holy women of old who hoped in God. So a gentle and quiet spirit never means putting up with intimidation. This quietness is rooted in God, not in her husband’s moods. A wife who is secure in God can speak the truth gently, and can also seek help for her own and her family’s safety when necessary.
q: Lately, what has most easily stirred up the lake of my heart, making me anxious, sharp, or cold?
Husbands: How can I pray for my wife, and become someone who brings her peace rather than tension?
talk: When do you think I’m most at peace? What is the atmosphere in our home like at those times?
What recent “storm” in our home could we hand over to the Lord together, instead of blaming each other? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down one thing you’d like to say to them gently.)
acts: When you feel like losing your temper, take a deep breath and silently pray, “Lord, speak to my heart: Peace, be still”
Husbands: Pray for your wife: “Lord, give her your peace”
Today, say one heartfelt thing to your spouse in a gentle tone
lessons.noon: “which is very precious in God’s sight” — Lord, right now make me gentle and quiet within, at rest in you.

lessons.title: Building Up or Tearing Down
lessons.theme: A home is built with wisdom, one brick at a time

v: Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.
Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established;
by knowledge the rooms are filled with all rare and beautiful treasure.

lessons.still: Look around the home you’re in: the walls, the table and chairs, every corner. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, today, were my words and attitude building up this home, or tearing it down?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The hand that tears down is often the hand of the self-ruled life: I want to be seen, I want to win, I want him to change. The hand that builds is the self-emptied hand: it asks first what is best for this home. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; winning an argument over something while tearing down a wall is the worst bargain of all.
lessons.jesus: Martha was busy serving and distracted, and Jesus gently told her, “but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part” (Luke 10:42). Jesus wasn’t belittling service; he was reminding her that for a home to be built firmly, we must first sit at the Lord’s feet. Building the home with wisdom starts with drawing near to the Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord, unless you build the house, we labor in vain. Give wives wisdom from you to build this home with their words and actions; and give husbands hearts that treasure them and work alongside them. Wherever we have torn down with our own hands, forgive us and repair it, and build our home on you, our rock. Amen.
teach: “Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands” (Proverbs 14:1). Most chilling are the words “with her own hands.” What destroys a home is often not a typhoon from outside, but our own hands. A biting comparison, belittling your husband in front of family and friends, a long cold war: each is like knocking a brick out of the wall. Any one time may not seem like much, but over time, the wall falls.

On the other hand, “Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established” (Proverbs 24:3). Building also happens brick by brick: a word of thanks, a word of affirmation, a dinner prepared with care, a look that still believes in your husband when he has failed. Building doesn’t require anything earth-shattering, only laying one good brick every day. And “by knowledge the rooms are filled with all rare and beautiful treasure” (Proverbs 24:4). The true wealth of a home is mutual trust, laughter, and an atmosphere of godliness.

Where does this wisdom come from? Proverbs says again and again that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. A wise woman is not someone born perfect, but someone who keeps coming to God and lets his word shape her. Nor does she build alone: though this verse speaks to wives, the responsibility of building the home is shared by husband and wife. Husbands, the best way to partner with her is to notice and treasure every brick your wife lays, and to build the home on the rock together.
q: Looking back on this week, when were my hands or my mouth “tearing down”? What did my heart really want at that moment?
Husbands: What “good bricks” has my wife laid for this home lately? Have I noticed them and thanked her?
talk: What do you think is the strongest “wall” in our home? How was it built?
If we laid one new brick for our home together this month, what would you like it to be?
acts: Wives: Today, make a point of saying one word of affirmation to your husband
Husbands: Pray for your wife, and thank her specifically for one thing she does
When you notice yourself about to say something that tears down, pause for three seconds
lessons.noon: “Every wise woman builds her house” — Lord, right now let my mouth and my hands be used to build up my home.

lessons.title: The Wisdom of Abigail
lessons.theme: Submission is not blind obedience; wisdom is courageously doing good in the Lord

v: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail. This woman was intelligent and had a beautiful face; but the man was surly and evil in his doings. He was of the house of Caleb.

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two containers of wine, five sheep ready dressed, five seahs of parched grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go on before me. Behold, I am coming after you.” But she didn’t tell her husband, Nabal.
David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.

lessons.still: Pause for a moment and remember times in your life when you were caught in a dilemma. Tell the Lord: “Lord, when I don’t know what to do, give me wisdom and courage from above.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Abigail’s focus was not on how foolish Nabal was, nor on how wronged she felt, but on God’s will and on everyone’s lives. When we shift from a human perspective to God’s perspective, we can find a way through even in hard places. Wisdom isn’t about being cleverer than others; it is letting God be Lord within me.
lessons.jesus: When a crowd held stones ready to stone a woman, Jesus straightened up and said, “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her” (John 8:7). With one sentence, he defused an act of violence. Jesus’ wisdom was gentle yet powerful. He shows us that wisdom can prevent harm and protect life.
lessons.pray: All-wise God, thank you for the example of Abigail. Give wives wisdom that is both gentle and brave, knowing when to speak and how to speak; and give husbands humble, teachable hearts, willing to listen to their wives’ counsel. Protect our home from all folly and harm, and help us walk in your ways together. Amen.
teach: Abigail’s husband Nabal “was surly and evil in his doings” (1 Samuel 25:3). He insulted David’s men, and even his own servant said, “he is such a worthless fellow that one can’t speak to him” (1 Samuel 25:17). David set out with four hundred men to take revenge, and the lives of the whole household hung in the balance. Abigail neither blindly went along with her husband’s folly nor made a scene at home; she quickly prepared gifts and went in person to prevent bloodshed.

This story shows us that biblical submission has never meant blind obedience. Abigail submitted more deeply to God, so she protected her whole household and kept David from sinning. Afterward David said, “Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand” (1 Samuel 25:33). A wise wife sometimes needs the courage to say “no,” to keep the whole family walking in God’s ways.

Abigail’s wisdom also lay in her sense of timing and propriety. She spoke to David with humility and grace; when she got home and found her husband very drunk, she waited until the next morning, when he was sober, to tell him what had happened (1 Samuel 25:36–37). She didn’t hide things from him long-term; she chose the right moment to tell the truth. Wives today can learn from this: don’t argue when your husband’s emotions are running high; express yourself gently and clearly when things are calm. If his behavior already endangers the family’s safety, then like Abigail, protect life first, and seek help from a pastor and professionals.
q: In our home, is there something I’ve kept silent about out of fear of conflict, which actually needs to be spoken with wisdom and courage?
When do I usually choose to express a different opinion? Is it at a time when the other person can actually hear it?
talk: When we disagree, how and when would you most like me to tell you?
Husband shares: When has your wife used wisdom to help you avoid a mistake? Thank her. (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’d like to say to them.)
acts: Wives: Choose a calm moment to gently share a thought you’ve been holding in
Husbands: Pray for your wife: “Lord, give her the wisdom of Abigail”
Husbands: Thank your wife for a piece of good advice she once gave you
lessons.noon: “Blessed is your discretion” — Lord, right now give me wisdom that is gentle and brave.

lessons.title: The Worthy Woman Who Is Praised
lessons.theme: A life that fears the LORD is the most beautiful crown in the home

v: Who can find a worthy woman? For her value is far above rubies.
The heart of her husband trusts in her. He shall have no lack of gain.
She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.
Her children rise up and call her blessed. Her husband also praises her:
“Many women do noble things, but you excel them all.”
Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised.

lessons.still: Think about the unseen sacrifices in your home; perhaps they are yours, perhaps your spouse’s. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, you have seen it all.” Let your heart be comforted in being seen by him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The worthy woman is not a superwoman holding everything up by her own strength, but a woman who lets God reign. Her strength comes from fearing the LORD, so she has no need to compare herself with others. Self-emptied, she lives without limits: when she no longer lives to prove herself, she is free to bless her whole household.
lessons.jesus: A woman poured very expensive ointment on Jesus’ head. Those around her criticized her for wasting it, but Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me” (Mark 14:6). Jesus publicly affirmed a woman’s offering to him. He saw her and praised her, and husbands should learn to see and praise in the same way.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us to each other. Help wives fear you and see their worth in your eyes, with no need to compare themselves with others; and help husbands trust them, praise them, and pray for them. May our home stand firm because we fear you, and may you receive all the glory. Amen.
teach: “Who can find a worthy woman? For her value is far above rubies” (Proverbs 31:10). The Hebrew word behind “worthy” carries the sense of strength, courage, and character; the same word describes Ruth as “a worthy woman” (Ruth 3:11). Proverbs 31 is not an intimidating checklist of perfection for wives, but a portrait of a woman who fears God: she is hardworking, farsighted, and generous, speaks with wisdom, and shines both at home and in society.

At the heart of this portrait is trust: “The heart of her husband trusts in her” (Proverbs 31:11), and “She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life” (Proverbs 31:12). A wife who is trusted grows stronger, and a wife who is trustworthy makes the home more stable. This also reminds us that the wife in Scripture is not passive or voiceless: she manages, makes decisions, and helps the poor, and her gifts are used for God’s kingdom and for her household.

The poem reaches its climax in praise: “Her children rise up and call her blessed. Her husband also praises her” (Proverbs 31:28). And the reason for the praise is this: “a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). Husbands, this week’s assignment is to open your mouth and praise her. Wives, please remember that your worth is not in other people’s applause, but in the Lord’s eyes. Looking back on this week: submission in the Lord, a gentle and quiet spirit, building with wisdom, and courageously doing good are all rooted in the fear of the LORD.
q: Wives: Do I often use Proverbs 31 as a “perfect standard” to beat myself up? How can I see myself today from the perspective of fearing God?
Husbands: When did I last praise my wife specifically? How can I pray for her and praise her this week?
talk: Husband, name three “worthy” qualities you see in your wife; wife, quietly receive them without brushing them off.
Of this week’s lessons, which picture has most helped us understand each other better? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down the thanks you’d like to express to them.)
acts: Husbands: Today, praise your wife once in front of others
Husbands: Pray for your wife using Proverbs 31:30
Wives: Write down one beautiful thing God has done in you, and thank him
lessons.noon: “a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised” — Lord, right now I don’t rely on looks or performance; I only want to fear you.

44.title: Leaving Our Parents: Honor and Boundaries

mem.t: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.

s: Each draw a simple family tree. Share one good gift you’ve brought from your family of origin, and one old pattern you’d like to change.
Together, plan one concrete way to honor both sets of parents: a phone call, a card, or a visit. If your parents have passed away, remember them together with thanksgiving.
Agree on one shared principle for relating to your in-laws; write it down and confirm it with each other.
Hold hands and pray for both your families, asking the Lord to bless both households and to build up ours.

lessons.title: Honor: Giving Parents Their Due Weight
lessons.theme: Honoring our parents is lifelong; it doesn’t end when we marry

v: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you.
But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God.

lessons.still: Be still and think of your parents, or the people who raised you: their faces, their sacrifices, and perhaps the wounds they left you. Bring all of it to the Lord and say: “Lord, teach me to see them with your heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, things. Honoring our parents puts God’s will above our own emotions; honoring them together as a couple refuses to let “your family” versus “my family” divide “our” family. From a human perspective, we see our parents’ faults; from God’s perspective, we see their worth.
lessons.jesus: On the cross, in terrible agony, Jesus still saw his mother standing nearby and said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” (John 19:27). From that hour, the disciple took her into his own home. In his hardest moment, Jesus still arranged for his mother’s future care, fulfilling his duty as a son.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for giving us life through our parents. Help us give them their due weight in our hearts, and honor both sets of parents with gratitude and action. Heal the wounds we received in our families of origin; forgive us where we have failed our parents, and give us wisdom to make amends. Amen.
teach: The first four of the Ten Commandments concern God; the fifth turns to parents: “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12). The Hebrew root of “honor” carries the idea of weight: giving our parents their due weight in our hearts. This is also “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2). God puts honoring parents first among the commandments about people, because the family is the root of all relationships.

When we marry, we “leave” our father and mother, but leaving is not cutting them off, much less dishonoring them. As children, honoring meant obeying; as adults, honoring means respect, gratitude, and care. Paul says children should “learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents, for this is acceptable in the sight of God” (1 Timothy 5:4). Being there for aging parents and supporting them is the responsibility of adult children, one that husband and wife need to carry together rather than pushing it onto one of them.

Honoring parents is something husband and wife do together: I honor my parents, and I honor yours too. Picture a tree putting out a new branch: the branch grows in its own direction, yet remains grateful for the nourishment of its roots. Honor also has boundaries: honoring is not the same as obeying in everything, much less enduring insults, manipulation, or harm. If parents’ demands go against God’s ways or put the family in danger, we can still respectfully say “no,” and seek a pastor’s support when needed.
q: In my heart, is the “weight” I give my parents mostly gratitude, or mostly a sense of debt and resentment?
In honoring my spouse’s parents, am I doing my share, or do I often push the responsibility onto my spouse?
talk: What is the one thing you’re most thankful for about your parents? How can we express our thanks to them together?
What do both sets of parents most need from us right now? How can we divide the tasks? (If your parents have passed away, share one thing you most want to remember about them.)
acts: Today, call or text your parents to check in on them
Pray once for each of your spouse’s parents
Name one thing about your spouse’s parents that you can learn from
lessons.noon: “let them learn first to show piety toward their own family and to repay their parents” — Lord, right now I want to please you by honoring my parents.

lessons.title: “I Will Go”: Leaving Willingly
lessons.theme: Healthy leaving takes courage to go and the blessing of letting go

v: They called Rebekah, and said to her, “Will you go with this man?” She said, “I will go.”
They sent away Rebekah, their sister, with her nurse, Abraham’s servant, and his men.
They blessed Rebekah, and said to her, “Our sister, may you be the mother of thousands of ten thousands, and let your offspring possess the gate of those who hate them.”
Listen, daughter, consider, and turn your ear. Forget your own people, and also your father’s house.

lessons.still: Picture Rebekah standing at the door of her home, glancing back at the familiar house, then turning and saying, “I will go.” Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, what part of my heart has not truly walked out the door yet?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Sometimes we can’t leave because self is on the throne: I need my parents’ approval to feel secure, or I want to use my family of origin’s strength to overpower my spouse. When we let Jesus reign, our security comes from the Lord, and we no longer need to grasp for it from our parents or our spouse. Only the self-emptied are free to leave, and free to honor.
lessons.jesus: Someone told Jesus that his mother and brothers were outside looking for him. Jesus looked at those around him and said, “whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, and mother” (Mark 3:35). Jesus loved his family, but he didn’t let their expectations override his Father’s will. He shows us that loving our family and putting God first can go together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for leading us out of our parents’ homes to build a new one. Give us courage to truly put each other first in our hearts; and bless both sets of parents, giving them peace as they let go. May our security come not from people’s approval, but from your love. Amen.
teach: Rebekah’s family asked her, “Will you go with this man?” She answered, “I will go” (Genesis 24:58). With three short words, a young woman left her familiar home for the future God had prepared. Her family didn’t cling to her: “They blessed Rebekah” (Genesis 24:60). Healthy leaving takes courage on the children’s part to go, and willingness on the parents’ part to bless and let go.

The psalmist tells the bride, “Forget your own people, and also your father’s house” (Psalm 45:10). This doesn’t mean she should erase her family from memory, but that old ties should not hinder the building of the new home. “Leaving” today includes: on important decisions, talking as a couple first and then seeking our parents’ advice; not taking our spouse’s faults back to our family of origin to complain; becoming gradually independent financially and practically; and not letting our parents’ approval be the only standard for decisions in our home.

Leaving is also a gift to our parents. Think of flying a kite: if the string is pulled too tight, the kite can’t fly; if the string snaps, the kite crashes. Mature leaving has both connection and space. Children don’t need to feel guilty for building a new home, and parents can entrust their children to God. When both generations are in the Lord, “leaving” is not a loss, but blessing extending into a new household.
q: When making important decisions, what matters most to me: God’s will, my spouse’s thoughts, or my parents’ views?
Have I ever complained about my spouse to my parents, causing my spouse to be looked down on in my family of origin?
talk: When it comes to “leaving,” what do you think we’ve done best? Where could we do better? Please say it gently.
What shared principle could we agree on, such as “we discuss important decisions with each other first”?
acts: Today, when a decision comes up, first ask your spouse: “What do you think?”
Don’t list your spouse’s faults in front of your family of origin
Pray for both sets of parents, asking the Lord to bless them
lessons.noon: “Will you go with this man?” — Lord, right now I choose to follow you, and to walk with my spouse.

lessons.title: Wisdom Between In-Laws
lessons.theme: Respect each other, be willing to listen, and each return to your own place

v: Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.
Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went his way into his own land.

lessons.still: Think about your parents-in-law. When you picture their faces, what rises first in your heart: gratitude, tension, or distance? Quietly hand that feeling over to the Lord: “Lord, build peace between our two families.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: In-law conflicts are often two families’ “selves” wrestling: whose habits are right, whose way is better. Pride provokes pride, and then mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law, fathers-in-law and sons-in-law, all end up wounded; humility inspires humility, and only then can everyone win. Change begins with me: when I let go first, the other side often softens too.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus entered Peter’s house and heard that Peter’s mother-in-law was lying sick with a fever, “He came and took her by the hand and raised her up” (Mark 1:31). Jesus cared for his disciple’s in-law and healed her with his own hand. He shows us that our parents-in-law are people to love and serve, not outsiders to be managed.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, thank you for the families you have given us on both sides. Build respect and harmony between us and our in-laws; give us humble, teachable hearts, along with gentle and firm boundaries. Help us as husband and wife to be of one mind, speaking the truth in love, so that both families are blessed through our home. Amen.
teach: When Moses’ father-in-law Jethro came to visit, “Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, and bowed and kissed him. They asked each other of their welfare” (Exodus 18:7). Seeing Moses judging the people from morning till evening, Jethro spoke frankly: “The thing that you do is not good” (Exodus 18:17), and explained why: “the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone” (Exodus 18:18). Here is an elder who cared about his son-in-law and had wisdom to offer.

This passage teaches both generations a lesson. For the older generation: when Jethro offered advice, he first expressed his concern, then proposed a solution, and added, “God be with you” (Exodus 18:19), leaving the decision with Moses and God. For the younger generation: “Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law” (Exodus 18:24) and did not reject good advice to save face. When the younger are humble and teachable and the elders respect boundaries, in-law relationships become a win for both.

The last line matters too: “Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went his way into his own land” (Exodus 18:27). Once Jethro had given his advice, he went back to his own home; he didn’t stay on to run Moses’ camp. Healthy in-law relationships are like this: we can care and we can advise, but each returns to their own place. When dealing with in-laws, husband and wife should stand on the same side, each taking responsibility for communicating with their own parents and respectfully explaining “our” decisions.
q: Toward my spouse’s parents, do I hold any judgments or grievances I haven’t let go of?
When my spouse’s parents offer advice, am I more like Moses, listening first, or do I get defensive first?
talk: With both sets of parents, in what areas would you like me to stand with you more? In what areas would you like me to be more understanding toward them?
Could we agree on this principle: each of us takes responsibility for communicating with our own parents? Do you think it’s workable? Is there anything you’d add?
acts: Name one strength of your spouse’s parents, and thank your spouse for it
Prepare a small greeting for your spouse’s parents
Confirm with your spouse one shared principle for relating to your in-laws
lessons.noon: “Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law” — Lord, right now give me a heart that is humble and teachable, gentle and firm.

lessons.title: Wounds and Healing from Our Family of Origin
lessons.theme: Christ’s precious blood can redeem inherited patterns and turn harm into blessing

v: knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers,
but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ,
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.

lessons.still: Be still. Perhaps some childhood scenes come to mind, warm or painful. There’s no need to rush to analyze them. Just tell the Lord: “Lord, you know it all. I place where I come from into your hands.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The patterns of our family of origin are stubborn because they long ago became part of my “self.” Change your mindset and your life will change: when I admit, “This is my old pattern, not God’s design,” the Holy Spirit has room to work. When my focus is on Jesus, I am no longer a victim or a copy of my family of origin, but a new creation of God.
lessons.jesus: Seeing a man blind from birth, the disciples asked who had sinned. Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John 9:3). Jesus moved the focus from assigning blame for the past to what God is doing today.
lessons.pray: Lord our Redeemer, thank you for redeeming us with your precious blood from the useless way of life handed down from our fathers. We give you all of our family of origin, the good and the bad: bless and continue what is good; heal and transform what has hurt. Make us the generation that breaks old patterns and passes on blessing. Amen.
teach: Peter writes, “knowing that you were redeemed... from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18). Every family has things “handed down”: ways of talking, patterns of handling conflict, anxiety about money, ways of expressing love. Some are blessings; others are bondage. In marriage we often find ourselves unconsciously replaying our parents’ script, and it startles even us.

The good news is that we were redeemed “not with corruptible things like silver or gold... but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Our family of origin influences us, but it does not determine us, because Christ’s precious blood is more powerful than our bloodline. Picture a river: we can’t change the silt washing down from upstream, but God can set a filter in our stretch of the river, so that the water flowing on to the next generation runs clear.

Joseph, sold by his brothers, said to them years later, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Healing does not mean pretending the hurt never happened; it means understanding it anew under God’s sovereignty. Some wounds run very deep, such as having suffered violence, abuse, or severe control at home. Please don’t carry them alone. Seeking the support of a pastor and a professional counselor is wisdom, not weakness; and keeping a safe distance from someone who may still hurt you does not violate honoring your parents.
q: What reaction of mine in marriage have I later realized is “exactly like my dad (or my mom)”?
Is there a wound from my family of origin that I need to bring to the Lord, perhaps even seeking professional support for it?
talk: What is the best gift you’ve brought from your family of origin?
Which old pattern of mine would you be willing to gently help me change? Please start with “I’ve noticed…” rather than “You always…”.
acts: Write down one old pattern you want to end in your generation
Write down one good tradition you want to pass on
If you carry deep wounds, take the initiative this week to arrange a conversation with a pastor or counselor
lessons.noon: “but God meant it for good” — Lord, right now I believe you can turn harm into blessing.

lessons.title: Finally: The Heart of Every Relationship
lessons.theme: Like-mindedness, compassion, and humility sum up all our relationships

v: Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous,
not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing, knowing that you were called to this, that you may inherit a blessing.
Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

lessons.still: Look back over these past few months: from learning to listen and speaking the truth in love, to reconciliation, forgiveness, mutual submission, and boundaries. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for everything you’ve done in our relationship, even the smallest change.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Every relational difficulty is rooted in self on the throne; every way forward is found in the self-emptied life. Pride against pride wounds both; humility inspires humility, and both win. This isn’t just a set of techniques but a life: let Jesus reign in our relationship, and his life will flow through our home.
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times, yet the risen Jesus prepared breakfast for him by the sea, asked him three times whether he loved him, and entrusted him with this charge: “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16). Jesus mended a broken relationship with love and brought Peter back into his mission. This is the most beautiful model for every relationship: restoration first, then moving forward together.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us all the way as we learn to love each other. Make us like-minded and compassionate, tenderhearted and humble, not repaying evil for evil, but blessing instead. Complete every change you have already begun; and prepare our home to become a home that worships you and blesses others. Amen.
teach: After speaking to wives and husbands, Peter sums up in one sentence: “Finally, all of you be like-minded, compassionate, loving as brothers, tenderhearted, courteous” (1 Peter 3:8). This perfectly sums up our journey through the “Relationships” stage: being quick to listen, speaking the truth in love, speaking words that build up, going first to make peace, forgiving, submitting to one another, and respecting boundaries. All the methods come back, in the end, to a single heart.

Peter continues: “not rendering evil for evil or insult for insult; but instead blessing” (1 Peter 3:9). The biggest trap in marital conflict is “You did this to me, so I’ll do it to you.” Picture two people shoving each other on ice: they’ll only end up falling down together. Paul also says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). “If it is possible” acknowledges reality: peace takes two. But “as much as it is up to you” reminds us to do our own part first.

The lesson of this stage can be summed up in one sentence: change begins with me. I can’t control my spouse, but I can choose to listen first, speak truthfully first, apologize first, and bless first. I can’t change my family of origin, but I can set healthy boundaries in the Lord. Change from the inside out means life first, then relationships, then ministry. As our relationship is renewed in the Lord, in the next stage we can turn outward together and become a home that worships God and blesses others.
